Let $P$ be a set of primitive type labels. A formal type $\Gamma$ records a finitely supported amount function $\nu_\Gamma:P\to\mathbb R_{\ge0}$, not identically zero. Primitive generators have their unit amount function. Positive scaling, separated product, and thermal-join constructors retain distinct formal tags and obey

$$\nu_{s\Gamma}=s\nu_\Gamma,\qquad \nu_{\Gamma\otimes\Gamma'}=\nu_\Gamma+\nu_{\Gamma'}\qquad(s>0).$$

Separated and joined types are distinct constructors even when their amount functions agree. Permutation, reassociation, and scaled-splitting conventions preserve the amount function. Define the positive **bookkeeping weight** $w_\Gamma:=\sum_{p\in P}\nu_\Gamma(p)$, a finite sum over support. Thus $w_{s\Gamma}=s w_\Gamma$ and every product or join has weight $w_\Gamma+w_{\Gamma'}$. The optional empty unit has zero amount function and weight zero; it is represented only by the empty compound, not as a simple chart. These are formal amounts, not masses in kilograms or an empirical conservation law. The functions and pointwise operations use [[def-function-space]]; their finite-support convention and finite sums are those of [[def-tdmath-tagged-scalable-compound]] and [[lem-tdmath-compound-mass-well-defined]].

Let $I$ index the declared family of simple types $\Gamma_i$. For each simple type $\Gamma$ in that family, let $n_\Gamma\ge1$ and let $\Gamma\subset\mathbb R^{n_\Gamma+1}$ be nonempty, open and convex, with coordinates $x=(u,v)$. The notation for a type and its chart is shared, but each state has a distinct raw tag $(\Gamma,x)$. Scaled charts are distinct tagged copies $s\Gamma=\{sx:x\in\Gamma\}$ with coordinate transport $x\mapsto sx$; transported raw tags remain distinct from the original raw tags. Let $e_{(\Gamma,x)}$ be the unit point mass from [[def-tdmath-tagged-scalable-compound]]. The represented state is

$$\mathsf{J}_\Gamma(x):=w_\Gamma e_{(\Gamma,x)},\qquad m(\mathsf{J}_\Gamma(x))=w_\Gamma.$$

Write $\mathsf{J}(x):=\mathsf{J}_\Gamma(x)$ when $x$ already carries its type tag. All state notation in this framework's compound comparisons, including a bare $x$, denotes $\mathsf{J}_\Gamma(x)$; a raw unit point mass is always written $e_{(\Gamma,x)}$. A separated pair is addition of represented states, not a unit product tag. Nonnegative multiples are pointwise and zero terms are omitted. For an encoded compound $c$, its aggregate composition is the finite amount function

$$\nu(c):=\sum_{(\Gamma,x)\in\operatorname{supp}(c)}\frac{c(\Gamma,x)}{w_\Gamma}\nu_\Gamma;\qquad m(c)=\sum_{p\in P}\nu(c)(p).$$

Fix the formal interpretation $\Pi(c)$ as the finite separated preparation whose factor at each nonzero raw tag $(\Gamma,x)$ is the amount $c(\Gamma,x)/w_\Gamma$ of that typed state, using the declared coordinate scaling transport. The accessibility relation on coefficient maps is the pullback of the declared relation on these preparations. Merging or splitting repeated copies of the same preparation is reversible; permutation and reassociation preserve the preparation. Thus $\Pi(\mathsf{J}_{s\Gamma}(sx))$ and $\Pi(s\mathsf{J}_\Gamma(x))$ are the same declared scaled preparation and yield

$$\mathsf{J}_{s\Gamma}(sx)\sim s\mathsf{J}_\Gamma(x),$$

although their raw point masses have different tags and are not equal. This reversible transport commutes with finite composition, nested type constructors, and scaled splitting. It is part of the precise formal scaling interpretation, not a deduction about physical accessibility from coordinate multiplication. A physical use must adopt the stated preparation maps and accessibility assumptions; fixed-composition models compare only preparations with the same $\nu$, while a declared channel model may additionally compare different compositions of equal $m$.

A comparison $A\prec B$ is defined only when $m(A)=m(B)$, as in the coefficient-map supplier. Write $A\sim B$ when both directions hold, and $A\prec\prec B$ when only the forward direction holds. On any fixed simple type, dividing every represented state by the same positive constant $w_\Gamma$ gives its unit-point-mass comparison. Positive scaling and its inverse preserve and reflect order; whenever the required CH and reference hypotheses hold, the unit-state entropy theorem applies after that normalization. If $S$ represents unit-point-mass comparisons, the entropy of a represented state is $w_\Gamma S(x)$ and the entropy of a finite sum $\sum_j t_j\mathsf{J}_\Gamma(x_j)$ is $\sum_j t_j w_\Gamma S(x_j)$. No independent rescaling across different types is assumed without a calibrator.

The common relation satisfies A1–A6 on all equal-mass finite compounds: (A1) reflexivity; (A2) transitivity; (A3) if $A\prec B$, then $A+C\prec B+C$ for every compound $C$; (A4) if $A\prec B$, then $tA\prec tB$ for every $t>0$; (A5) $t\mathsf{J}_\Gamma(x)$ is equivalent to $s\mathsf{J}_\Gamma(x)+(t-s)\mathsf{J}_\Gamma(x)$ for $t>0$ and $0<s<t$, with the reversible scaled-copy transport above; (A6) for equal-mass $A,B$, fixed positive equal-mass spectators $Z_0,Z_1$, and every sequence $\epsilon_n>0$ decreasing to zero, $A+\epsilon_n Z_0\prec B+\epsilon_n Z_1$ for all $n$ implies $A\prec B$. These are hypotheses, not conclusions. No comparison hypothesis is included here.

For each $i$ and $x\in\Gamma_i$, define the forward sector $A_x:=\{y\in\Gamma_i:\mathsf{J}_{\Gamma_i}(x)\prec\mathsf{J}_{\Gamma_i}(y)\}$. The simple-domain assumptions are: (A7) for $x,y\in\Gamma_i$ and $0<t<1$, the encoded compound $t\mathsf{J}_{\Gamma_i}(x)+(1-t)\mathsf{J}_{\Gamma_i}(y)$ compares to $\mathsf{J}_{\Gamma_i}(tx+(1-t)y)$; both have bookkeeping mass $w_{\Gamma_i}$, and convexity puts the recombined coordinate in the chart; (S1) each $x$ has a strict successor; (S2) $A_x$ has exactly one supporting hyperplane at $x$, expressible as $u-u_x+P_i(x)\cdot(v-v_x)=0$ with a finite-valued slope map $P_i:\Gamma_i\to\mathbb R^{n_i}$, and $P_i$ is locally Lipschitz; (S3) the boundary of $A_x$ relative to $\Gamma_i$ is arcwise connected. A supporting hyperplane means that $A_x$ lies in one of its closed half-spaces and meets the plane at $x$. The affine hull is the smallest affine subspace containing a set; relative interior is interior in that affine hull. Closure and boundary are taken in the indicated affine hull or in $\Gamma_i$, as named; boundary is closure intersected with closure of the complement in that relative topology.

This definition imposes no physical interpretation, units, or empirical claim. A contact theorem that uses joins must separately assume that each join is a simple domain satisfying these same forward-sector hypotheses.

Under [[def-tdmath-forward-sector-hypotheses]], for every simple state $x$, the forward sector $A_x=\{y\in\Gamma_i:x\prec y\}$ is convex and closed relative to $\Gamma_i$. For collinear $y=tx+(1-t)z$, $0<t<1$, $y\prec z$ implies $x\prec y$, and $x\prec z$ implies $x\prec y$.
Under [[def-tdmath-forward-sector-hypotheses]], every forward sector $A_x$ has nonempty interior in its ambient simple domain $\Gamma_i$.

Let $C$ be a nonempty convex set in a finite-dimensional affine Euclidean space $H$ of dimension $k\ge1$, let $\operatorname{aff}C=H$, and put $K=\overline{C}^{\,H}$. If $z\in\partial_H K$ (that is, $z\in K$ and every relative neighborhood of $z$ meets $H\setminus K$), then there is a nonzero linear functional $\ell$ on the translation space of $H$ such that $\ell(q-z)\le0$ for all $q\in C$. If $C\subset\mathbb R^d$ has affine dimension at most $d-2$, then every $z\in C$ has at least two distinct ambient supporting hyperplanes containing $\operatorname{aff}C$.

Let $K\subset\mathbb R^d$ be closed and convex with nonempty interior, $d\ge1$, and let $x\in\partial K$. Suppose $K$ has exactly one supporting hyperplane at $x$. Choose its inward unit normal $n$, so $n\cdot(q-x)\ge0$ for every $q\in K$. Then for every $v$ with $n\cdot v>0$, there is $\delta>0$ such that $x+tv\in\operatorname{int}K$ for every $0<t<\delta$.

Let $U\subset\mathbb R^d$ be open and convex, and let $f:U\to\mathbb R$ be finite and convex, meaning $f((1-t)x+ty)\le(1-t)f(x)+tf(y)$ for every $x,y\in U$ and $t\in[0,1]$. For every $x_0\in U$, there are a neighborhood $V$ of $x_0$ and $L<\infty$ such that $|f(x)-f(y)|\le L\|x-y\|$ for all $x,y\in V$. The same conclusion holds for finite concave functions by applying the result to $-f$.
Let $L\ge0$, $T>0$, and let $f:[0,T]\to[0,\infty)$ be continuous. If $f(t)\le L\int_0^t f(s)\,ds$ for every $t\in[0,T]$, then $f(t)=0$ for every $t\in[0,T]$.

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$ with $n \ge 1$, let $\mathbb{R}^n$ be the set of functions
$n \to \mathbb{R}$ and let $d_2$ be the Euclidean metric on it
([[lem-metrics-on-rn]]). Then:

1. **Closed boxes are compact.** For reals $a_k \le b_k$ $(k < n)$ the box
   $Q = \{\, x \in \mathbb{R}^n : a_k \le x_k \le b_k \text{ for every } k < n \,\}$
   is a compact subset of $(\mathbb{R}^n, d_2)$ ([[def-metric-compactness]]).
2. **Heine-Borel.** A subset $K \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ is a compact subset of
   $(\mathbb{R}^n, d_2)$ if and only if $K$ is closed in $\mathbb{R}^n$
   ([[def-metric-topology]]) and bounded
   ([[def-metric-bounded-diameter]]).
3. **The real line.** A subset $K \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ is a compact subset of
   $(\mathbb{R}, d_{\mathbb{R}})$, the usual metric $d_{\mathbb{R}}(x,y) = |x-y|$
   ([[lem-real-line-is-a-metric-space]]), if and only if $K$ is closed in
   $\mathbb{R}$ and bounded.

**No choice principle is used.** The bisection below halves one coordinate at a
time and takes the **left** half whenever the left half still fails to be finitely
covered, the right half otherwise: a rule with two outcomes, decided by a
property of the box, not a selection. That is the whole reason the theorem is
available in ZF, while the general "complete and totally bounded implies compact"
([[thm-complete-and-totally-bounded-implies-compact]]) is not.

The hypothesis $n \ge 1$ is inherited from [[lem-metrics-on-rn]], which defines
$\mathbb{R}^n$ and its metrics only there; the last remark below records what
happens at $n = 0$.

Let $A, B \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ with
$g[A] \subseteq B$ and let $f : B \to \mathbb{R}$, so that the composite
$f \circ g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ is defined. Let $c \in A$ be a limit point of
$A$ ([[def-limit-point-r]]) at which $g$ is differentiable
([[def-derivative]]), put $b := g(c)$, and suppose $b$ is a limit point of $B$
at which $f$ is differentiable. Then $f \circ g$ is differentiable at $c$ and

$$(f \circ g)'(c) \;=\; f'\bigl(g(c)\bigr)\,g'(c) .$$

**Both limit-point hypotheses are needed, and neither is automatic.** That $c$
is a limit point of $A$ is what makes $g'(c)$ and $(f \circ g)'(c)$ defined
symbols; that $b = g(c)$ is a limit point of $B$ is what makes $f'(b)$ one.
Nothing forces the second: $g$ may be differentiable at $c$ and send $c$ to an
isolated point of $B$, and there $f'(b)$ is not defined and the formula asserts
nothing.

**No case analysis appears anywhere.** The naive difference-quotient proof
writes $\frac{f(g(x)) - f(g(c))}{g(x) - g(c)} \cdot \frac{g(x) - g(c)}{x - c}$
and then has to say what happens where $g(x) = g(c)$, which may occur at points
arbitrarily close to $c$. Carathéodory's factorisation never divides by the
inner increment, so the difficulty does not arise.

Let $a<b$. Suppose $G:[a,b]\to\mathbb R$ is continuous on $[a,b]$ and differentiable on $(a,b)$. If $f:[a,b]\to\mathbb R$ is Riemann integrable and

$$f(x)=G'(x)\qquad(a<x<b),$$

then

$$\int_a^b f=G(b)-G(a).$$

No derivative of $G$ at either endpoint is assumed, and the two endpoint values assigned to the integrable extension $f$ do not enter the conclusion.

Let $a < b$ be reals and let $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be continuous on $[a,b]$
([[def-continuity-real]]). Then $f$ is bounded ([[def-bounded-set]]) and Riemann
integrable on $[a,b]$ ([[def-darboux-integral]]).

**The proof gives more than integrability: it gives a partition that works.** For
every real $\varepsilon > 0$ the uniform partition into $N$ parts already
satisfies $U(f,P) - L(f,P) < \varepsilon$, as soon as $N$ is large enough that
$(b-a)/\iota(N)$ is below the $\delta$ that uniform continuity supplies for
$\varepsilon/\bigl(2(b-a)\bigr)$. Uniform continuity is exactly what makes one
$\delta$ serve all $N$ subintervals at once, and it is the only place where the
compactness of $[a,b]$ is used.

Let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ be open, let $a\in U$, and let $f:U\to\mathbb R^n$. The map $f$ is **totally differentiable at $a$** when there is a linear map $L:\mathbb R^m\to\mathbb R^n$ ([[def-euclidean-linear-map]]) such that

$$\lim_{h\to0}\frac{\|f(a+h)-f(a)-Lh\|_2}{\|h\|_2}=0,$$

where the quotient is considered for $h\ne0$ with $a+h\in U$. The map $L$, when it exists, is denoted $Df(a)$ and called the **total derivative**. Equivalently, $f(a+h)=f(a)+Df(a)h+r(h)$ with $\|r(h)\|_2/\|h\|_2\to0$.

Let $k\in\mathbb N$, let $m,q\ge1$, let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ be open, and let $f:U\to\mathbb R^q$. A map $f:U\to\mathbb R^q$ is of class $C^k$ when each component is of class $C^k$. Each scalar component uses the word-derivative convention of [[def-ck-and-multi-index-notation-in-several-variables]], whose source dimension is positive. The map is **smooth**, or $C^\infty$, when it is $C^k$ for every $k\in\mathbb N$.

Let $n\ge1$ and let $U,V\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open. A bijection $f:U\to V$ is a **$C^k$ diffeomorphism** when both $f$ and $f^{-1}$ are $C^k$. For $k\ge1$, a **local $C^k$ diffeomorphism at $a\in U$** is a restriction $f|_P:P\to Q$ between open neighbourhoods of $a$ and $f(a)$ that is a $C^k$ diffeomorphism. At $k=1$ this agrees with [[def-c-one-map-and-local-inverse]]: continuous first partial derivatives give the required total derivative by [[thm-continuous-partial-derivatives-imply-total-differentiability]], while continuity of the total derivative gives continuity of its matrix entries and hence of the first partial derivatives.

Let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ be open and let $f:U\to\mathbb R^n$. Suppose every partial derivative $\partial_jf$ exists on a neighbourhood of $a\in U$ and is continuous at $a$. Then $f$ is totally differentiable at $a$, and $Df(a)$ is the linear map with matrix $Jf(a)$.

Let $f:U\to V\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be totally differentiable at $a\in U$ and let $g:V\to\mathbb R^p$ be totally differentiable at $f(a)$. Then $g\circ f$ is totally differentiable at $a$ and

$$D(g\circ f)(a)=Dg(f(a))\circ Df(a).$$

derivations.claim: For fixed $x=(u_x,v_x)$, the vertical section $I_x:=\{u:(u,v_x)\in A_x\}$ is a relatively closed convex interval by [F1]. The support plane at $x$ confines it to one side of $u_x$. Its inward normal has nonzero energy component, so [F4] gives a nontrivial interior vertical segment on that side.

The fiber orientation is locally constant in $v$. At any $x$, choose one vertical point just inside the supported half-space and one just outside; by [F4] the inside point can be chosen in $\operatorname{int}A_x$. Openness of $\Gamma_i$ and of the interior and exterior regions preserves these memberships on nearby fibers. Each such fiber therefore meets $\partial A_x$ between these two energy values. A support of $A_x$ at that boundary point also supports the point's own sector and so has its S2 orientation; the inside/outside placement fixes that orientation. Thus nearby fibers have the same sign as the fiber through $x$. Since $\Gamma_i$ is convex, it is connected; a locally constant two-valued sign is constant.

Let $u,w$ be two $C^1$ graph solutions of $Dq=-P_i(q,v)$ on a common open domain, and suppose $u(v_0)=w(v_0)$. Since $P_i$ is locally Lipschitz, choose a convex neighborhood of $(u(v_0),v_0)$ on which one Lipschitz constant $L$ works. Continuity of $u,w$ lets us choose a convex ball about $v_0$ whose closure lies in the common domain and whose two graph images stay in that neighborhood; take any $v$ in a smaller concentric ball. Put $d=v-v_0$ and $\gamma(t)=v_0+td$ for $0\le t\le1$. By [F8], $r(t)=u(\gamma(t))-w(\gamma(t))$ is $C^1$ and
$r'(t)=[-P_i(u(\gamma(t)),\gamma(t))+P_i(w(\gamma(t)),\gamma(t))]\cdot d.$
The local Lipschitz bound for $P_i$ gives $|r'(t)|\le L\|d\||r(t)|$. The derivative is continuous, hence integrable by [F10]; [F9] gives $r(t)=\int_0^t r'(s)\,ds$; hence $h(t):=|r(t)|\le L\|d\|\int_0^t h(s)\,ds$. Apply [F6] on $[0,1]$ to obtain $h=0$. Thus $u=w$ near $v_0$. Along any polygonal path in the common open domain, the set of path parameters at which equality holds is closed by continuity and open by this local result; since the path interval is connected and the set is nonempty, equality holds along the whole path. Every open connected subset of Euclidean space is polygonally connected: points reachable from a fixed point by finitely many segments in small balls form a nonempty relatively open and relatively closed set. Therefore equality extends throughout each common connected domain.

The convex, relatively closed interval $I_x$ contains a nontrivial segment on the inward side by step 1.1 and [F4]. Suppose it does not contain the whole open $\Gamma_i$-fiber on that side. Its endpoint $b$ toward that side then lies inside $\Gamma_i$; relative closedness puts $b$ in $I_x$, so the interval from $x$ to $b$ is a compact nondegenerate interval by [F7]. Let $x_1$ be its midpoint. Since $x_1\in A_x$, transitivity gives $A_{x_1}\subseteq A_x$. The supporting plane of $A_{x_1}$ has nonzero energy coefficient, so its vertical section lies wholly on one side of $x_1$; being contained in $I_x$, it lies in one half of $[x,b]$ and has at most half its length. It is nonempty and closed relative to $[x,b]$, hence compact. Repeat: take the midpoint $x_{k+1}$ of the current compact interval $I_{x_k}$; then $x_k\prec x_{k+1}$, so the next section is nested inside the current one and again has at most half its length. These intervals have nonempty total intersection: otherwise their open complements would cover the first compact interval, a finite subcover would do so by [F7], and nesting would make one interval empty. Their lengths tend to zero, so the intersection has a unique point $x_\infty$, still in the first interval contained in $\Gamma_i$. The midpoint recursion and this unique intersection require no selection from an arbitrary countable family. Relative closedness puts $x_\infty$ in every $A_{x_k}$, hence $A_{x_\infty}\subseteq A_{x_k}$ by transitivity. Its vertical section is therefore only $\{x_\infty\}$, contradicting the nontrivial interior vertical segment at $x_\infty$ supplied by [F4]. Thus $I_x$ contains the whole open fiber on its inward side.

All states on a fixed work-coordinate fiber have the same orientation. If $x$ is oriented upward and a state $z$ above it were oriented downward, the full upward section from step 2.1 gives $x\prec z$, and the full downward section from $z$ gives $z\prec w$ for a state $w$ below $x$, contradicting the support at $x$. If a state $y$ below an upward $x$ were oriented downward, choose $z$ above $x$ with $x\prec z$; the first collinear implication in [F1], applied to $x$ between $y$ and $z$, gives $y\prec x$, contradicting the downward support at $y$. The reversed argument handles a downward $x$.
Adopt the coordinate convention $\varepsilon_i=1$. Step 2.1 and the common orientation give $x\prec y$ exactly for $u_y\ge u_x$ at fixed $v$, with strict comparison for $u_y>u_x$.

Put $\rho_x=\pi_v(\partial A_x)$. At a boundary point $z\in\partial A_x$, [F3] supplies a support to $A_x$. Because $A_z\subseteq A_x$, that plane also supports $A_z$ and equals its unique S2 plane. Its finite slope gives a nonvertical inward direction; [F4] supplies nearby vertical points inside $A_x$, while the opposite side is outside by the support. Neighborhoods of one inside and one outside point show every nearby work fiber meets $\partial A_x$. Hence $\rho_x$ is open. It is connected because S3 makes $\partial A_x$ arcwise connected and projection is continuous. By step 4.1, every vertical fiber over $\rho_x$ has exactly one boundary energy; call it $u_x(v)$.

For $v,v'\in\rho_x$, convexity of $A_x$ puts every convex combination of their boundary states in $A_x$. On any sufficiently small convex ball in $\rho_x$, the unique-boundary property and upward orientation make $u_x$ the least energy in each fiber. Therefore $u_x(tv+(1-t)v')\le t u_x(v)+(1-t)u_x(v')$, so $u_x$ is finite and convex there. It is locally Lipschitz by [F5]. The inward support at $(u_x(v),v)$ gives
$u_x(v')-u_x(v)\ge -P_i(u_x(v),v)\cdot(v'-v).$
The support at $(u_x(v'),v')$ gives
$u_x(v')-u_x(v)\le -P_i(u_x(v'),v')\cdot(v'-v).$
Local Lipschitz continuity of $u_x$ and $P_i$ makes the difference between these linear bounds $O(\|v'-v\|^2)$. Thus $u_x$ is differentiable with derivative $-P_i(u_x(v),v)$, and that derivative is locally Lipschitz. Hence $u_x\in C^1$ with locally Lipschitz derivative.

If $y\in\partial A_x$, then $A_y\subseteq A_x$. The boundary graphs agree at $v_y$ and solve the same differential equation. The set of $v\in\rho_y$ where $v\in\rho_x$ and $u_y(v)=u_x(v)$ is nonempty, open by step 1.3, and closed by continuity and relative closedness of $\partial A_x$. Connectedness of $\rho_y$ makes it all of $\rho_y$. This shows $\rho_y\subseteq\rho_x$. The same argument, using relative closedness of $\partial A_y$, shows $\rho_y$ is relatively closed in connected $\rho_x$; it is relatively open because both projections are open. Hence $\rho_x=\rho_y$ and the boundary graphs agree. In particular $x\in\partial A_y$, so $y\prec x$; together with $y\in A_x$ and transitivity this gives $A_x=A_y$.

citations.quote: A measure space is a triple $(X,\Sigma,\mu)$ where $\Sigma$ contains $\varnothing,X$ and is closed under complements and countable unions (a $\sigma$-algebra) of subsets of $X$ and $\mu:\Sigma\to[0,\infty]$ is countably additive with $\mu(\varnothing)=0$. A measurable function $f:X\to[-\infty,\infty]$ has measurable inverse images of Borel sets, where $[-\infty,\infty]$ has its order topology: finite open intervals and the endpoint neighborhoods $[-\infty,a)$ and $(a,\infty]$ form a basis. Its Borel sigma-algebra is generated by these open sets. A complex-valued function is measurable exactly when its finite real and imaginary parts are measurable, equivalently for the usual Borel structure of $\mathbb C$. Almost-everywhere assertions mean outside a measurable $\mu$-null set; completeness of $\mu$ is not assumed. Nonnegative extended addition uses $a+\infty=\infty+a=\infty$ for $a\in[0,\infty]$; positive scalars multiply $\infty$ to $\infty$, while $0\cdot\infty=0$. Signed expressions $\infty-\infty$ remain undefined and are not used in signed integrals. A nonnegative simple function has the form $s=\sum_{j=1}^m c_j\mathbf1_{A_j}$ with finitely many disjoint $A_j\in\Sigma$ and finite $c_j\ge0$. Define $c\mu(A)=+\infty$ if $c>0$ and $\mu(A)=+\infty$, define $0\cdot\infty:=0$, and define the finite sum of these extended nonnegative terms to be $+\infty$ if any term is $+\infty$ and otherwise the real finite sum of [[def-finite-sum]]. Then $\int s\,d\mu:=\sum_j c_j\mu(A_j)$; using canonical level sets $\{s=c\}$ makes this value representation-independent. For measurable $f\ge0$, define $\int f\,d\mu:=\sup\{\int s\,d\mu: s\text{ is simple and }0\le s\le f\}$, using [[def-complete-ordered-field]] for a bounded set of finite values and setting the supremum to $+\infty$ when the values are unbounded or one is infinite. A real measurable $f$ is integrable when $\int|f|\,d\mu<\infty$, and then $\int f:=\int f^+-\int f^-$, where $f^+=\max(f,0)$ and $f^-:=\max(-f,0)$. Complex integrability and integration are defined by integrable real and imaginary parts.

Let $(X,\Sigma,\mu)$ be a measure space and let $f_n:X\to\mathbb C$ be measurable with $f_n\to f$ almost everywhere. Suppose $g\ge0$ is measurable and $\int g\,d\mu<\infty$, and $|f_n|\le g$ almost everywhere for every $n$. Let $f_0(x)$ be the finite complex pointwise limit of $(f_n(x))$ where it exists, and $0$ elsewhere. Then $f_0$ is measurable, equals $f$ almost everywhere, is integrable, and $\int f_n\,d\mu\to\int f_0\,d\mu$ and $\int|f_n-f_0|\,d\mu\to0$. If the specified $f$ is measurable, these same conclusions hold with $f$ in place of $f_0$. In particular this is automatic when $\mu$ is complete. On a noncomplete measure space an arbitrary almost-everywhere representative need not be measurable, so no integral of such a nonmeasurable $f$ is asserted.

For $x\in\mathbb R$, define
$$\exp(x):=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\frac{x^n}{\iota(n!)}, \qquad e:=\exp(1),$$
provided by the all-real convergence proved in [[lem-exponential-series-has-infinite-radius]]. Here $n!\in\mathbb N$ is the factorial of [[def-factorial-and-falling-factorial]], $\iota(n!)$ is its nonzero real image ([[def-canonical-natural]], [[lem-of-naturals-positive]]), and powers and series are those of [[def-integer-power]] and [[def-series]].

This is a real power series centred at $0$ ([[def-real-power-series-and-radius-of-convergence]]). No logarithm, irrational power, or differential equation enters the definition.

The real exponential function is $C^\infty$, and for every $m\in\mathbb N$,
$$\exp^{(m)}=\exp.$$
In particular $(\exp)'=\exp$.

For $x>0$, define $\log x$ to be the unique real $y$ such that $\exp(y)=x$. This is well-defined because [[cor-exponential-is-a-bijection-onto-positive-reals]] states that $\exp:\mathbb R\to(0,\infty)$ is a bijection.

Thus $\log:(0,\infty)\to\mathbb R$ is the inverse function of $\exp$. In particular, $\log(\exp y)=y$ for every $y\in\mathbb R$ and $\exp(\log x)=x$ for every $x>0$.

For $x>0$, $\log$ is differentiable and
$$\log'(x)=\frac1x,\qquad \log x=\int_1^x\frac{dt}{t}.$$

Let $a, b \in \mathbb{R}$ with $a < b$ and let $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be
continuous on $[a,b]$ ([[def-continuity-real]], [[def-interval]]) and
differentiable at every point of $(a,b)$ as a function on $[a,b]$
([[def-derivative]]). Then there is $c \in (a,b)$ with

$$f(b) - f(a) \;=\; f'(c)\,(b - a) .$$

Equivalently, since $b - a \ne 0$, there is $c \in (a,b)$ at which
$f'(c) = \bigl(f(b)-f(a)\bigr)/(b-a)$: the derivative somewhere inside equals
the average rate of change across the whole interval.

**Continuity on the closed interval cannot be dropped.** Differentiability at
every point of $(a,b)$ alone does not suffice: a function on $[0,1]$,
differentiable at every point of $(0,1)$ with derivative constantly $1$, for
which no $c$ works, is exhibited later on this page as a false statement, and
the companion page works the same witness out in full.

Let $A, B \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ with
$g[A] \subseteq B$ and let $f : B \to \mathbb{R}$, so that the composite
$f \circ g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ is defined. Let $c \in A$ be a limit point of
$A$ ([[def-limit-point-r]]) at which $g$ is differentiable
([[def-derivative]]), put $b := g(c)$, and suppose $b$ is a limit point of $B$
at which $f$ is differentiable. Then $f \circ g$ is differentiable at $c$ and

$$(f \circ g)'(c) \;=\; f'\bigl(g(c)\bigr)\,g'(c) .$$

**Both limit-point hypotheses are needed, and neither is automatic.** That $c$
is a limit point of $A$ is what makes $g'(c)$ and $(f \circ g)'(c)$ defined
symbols; that $b = g(c)$ is a limit point of $B$ is what makes $f'(b)$ one.
Nothing forces the second: $g$ may be differentiable at $c$ and send $c$ to an
isolated point of $B$, and there $f'(b)$ is not defined and the formula asserts
nothing.

**No case analysis appears anywhere.** The naive difference-quotient proof
writes $\frac{f(g(x)) - f(g(c))}{g(x) - g(c)} \cdot \frac{g(x) - g(c)}{x - c}$
and then has to say what happens where $g(x) = g(c)$, which may occur at points
arbitrarily close to $c$. Carathéodory's factorisation never divides by the
inner increment, so the difficulty does not arise.

Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $c \in A$ be a limit point of $A$
([[def-limit-point-r]]), let $f, g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ be differentiable at $c$
([[def-derivative]]) and let $\alpha \in \mathbb{R}$. Then:

1. $f + g$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(f+g)'(c) = f'(c) + g'(c)$;
2. $\alpha f$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(\alpha f)'(c) = \alpha f'(c)$;
3. $fg$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(fg)'(c) = f'(c)g(c) + f(c)g'(c)$;
4. if $g(c) \ne 0$ then, writing $A_0 := \{\, x \in A : g(x) \ne 0 \,\}$, the
   point $c$ lies in $A_0$ and is a limit point of $A_0$, the quotient
   $(f/g)|_{A_0} : A_0 \to \mathbb{R}$, $x \mapsto f(x)/g(x)$, is differentiable
   at $c$ as a function on $A_0$, and
   $$\bigl((f/g)|_{A_0}\bigr)'(c) \;=\; \frac{f'(c)\,g(c) - f(c)\,g'(c)}{g(c)^{2}} .$$

Each claim asserts two things: that the derivative on the left exists, and that
it has the stated value. Both are proved.

**Why claim 4 is stated on $A_0$.** The function $f/g$ is not defined where $g$
vanishes, and $g$ may vanish at points of $A$ far from $c$; restricting to $A_0$
is forced. That the restriction still has $c$ as a limit point, so that a
derivative there means anything at all, is not free either, and it is the last
claim of [[lem-sign-preservation-near-a-limit]] applied to $g$. The hypothesis
is $g(c) \ne 0$, not "$g$ vanishes nowhere".

**Everything is proved through
[[thm-caratheodory-characterisation]].** No difference quotient is estimated and
no limit theorem beyond continuity is used, so no choice principle is spent.
The four identities are four algebraic rearrangements of an increment, each
followed by a reading of [[thm-algebra-of-continuous-functions]].

Let $(X,\mathcal{A})$, $(Y,\mathcal{B})$, and $(Z,\mathcal{C})$ be measurable
spaces. If $f : (X,\mathcal{A}) \to (Y,\mathcal{B})$ is measurable and
$g : (Y,\mathcal{B}) \to (Z,\mathcal{C})$ is measurable, then
$g \circ f : (X,\mathcal{A}) \to (Z,\mathcal{C})$ is measurable.

In particular, if $f$ is measurable and $g$ is a Borel measurable function on
its codomain, then $g \circ f$ is measurable.

derivations.claim: For each fixed parameter, measurable energy/observable coordinates and [F7] make every finite linear combination, exponential weight, weighted first/second moment and parameter difference quotient measurable; their displayed pointwise derivative limits are the same measurable compositions. For a coordinate direction $a$, the difference quotient of $w e^{\theta\cdot X}$ tends pointwise to $wX_a e^{\theta\cdot X}$. On a compact neighborhood $K'$ of $\theta$, the mean-value theorem [F5] bounds its absolute value by $w|X_a|e^{\eta\cdot X}$ for an intermediate parameter $\eta\in K'$, at most $G_{K'}$. Dominated convergence [F2] therefore gives $\partial_aZ=\int wX_a e^{\theta\cdot X}d\mu$. Applying the same argument to the first-moment numerator gives $\partial_b\int wX_a e^{\theta\cdot X}d\mu=\int wX_aX_b e^{\theta\cdot X}d\mu$; the same envelope controls this quotient because $|X_aX_b|\le1+\sum_c|X_c|^2$.

Divide the first derivative by $Z>0$ and use [F4] to obtain $\partial_a\log Z=\mathbb E_\theta X_a$. The quotient rule for the normalized first moment gives $\partial_b\mathbb E_\theta X_a=\mathbb E_\theta(X_aX_b)-\mathbb E_\theta X_a\mathbb E_\theta X_b$, the covariance.
For any $v\in\mathbb R^r$, $v^T(\nabla^2\log Z)v=\mathbb E_\theta[(v\cdot X-\mathbb E_\theta(v\cdot X))^2]\ge0$. This proves positive semidefiniteness without any independence assumption.

case_scope.source_excerpt: Let $(X,\Sigma,\mu)$ be a measure space, let $w:X\to[0,\infty)$ and $X_a:X\to\mathbb R$ ($1\le a\le r$) be measurable, and let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^r$ be open. For $\theta=(\theta_1,\ldots,\theta_r)$, define $\theta\cdot X(x):=\sum_{a=1}^r\theta_aX_a(x)$. Set $Z(\theta):=\int w\exp(\theta\cdot X)\,d\mu$ and assume $0<Z(\theta)<\infty$ on $U$. Suppose for every compact $K\subset U$ there is an integrable $G_K\ge0$ such that $w e^{\theta\cdot X}(1+\sum_a|X_a|^2)\le G_K$ pointwise for all $\theta\in K$. For the normalized density $p_\theta=w e^{\theta\cdot X}/Z(\theta)$, define $\mathbb E_\theta Y:=\int Yp_\theta\,d\mu$ when integrable and $\operatorname{Cov}_\theta(X_a,X_b):=\mathbb E_\theta[(X_a-\mathbb E_\theta X_a)(X_b-\mathbb E_\theta X_b)]$. Then $\partial_a\log Z=\mathbb E_\theta X_a$ and $\partial_b\mathbb E_\theta X_a=\operatorname{Cov}_\theta(X_a,X_b)$. Thus the Hessian of $\log Z$ is positive semidefinite. This is a mathematical model identity; it assumes no independence or absence of correlations.

supplier_excerpts.exact_statement: A measure space is a triple $(X,\Sigma,\mu)$ where $\Sigma$ contains $\varnothing,X$ and is closed under complements and countable unions (a $\sigma$-algebra) of subsets of $X$ and $\mu:\Sigma\to[0,\infty]$ is countably additive with $\mu(\varnothing)=0$. A measurable function $f:X\to[-\infty,\infty]$ has measurable inverse images of Borel sets, where the Borel sets of the extended real line are the sigma-algebra generated by its open sets. A nonnegative simple function has the form $s=\sum_{j=1}^m c_j\mathbf1_{A_j}$ with finitely many disjoint $A_j\in\Sigma$ and finite $c_j\ge0$. Define $c\mu(A)=+\infty$ if $c>0$ and $\mu(A)=+\infty$, define $0\cdot\infty:=0$, and define the finite sum of these extended nonnegative terms to be $+\infty$ if any term is $+\infty$ and otherwise the real finite sum of [[def-finite-sum]]. Then $\int s\,d\mu:=\sum_j c_j\mu(A_j)$; using canonical level sets $\{s=c\}$ makes this value representation-independent. For measurable $f\ge0$, define $\int f\,d\mu:=\sup\{\int s\,d\mu: s\text{ is simple and }0\le s\le f\}$, using [[def-complete-ordered-field]] for a bounded set of finite values and setting the supremum to $+\infty$ when the values are unbounded or one is infinite. A real measurable $f$ is integrable when $\int|f|\,d\mu<\infty$, and then $\int f:=\int f^+-\int f^-$, where $f^+=\max(f,0)$ and $f^-:=\max(-f,0)$. Complex integrability and integration are defined by integrable real and imaginary parts.

For $x\in\mathbb R$, define
$$\exp(x):=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\frac{x^n}{\iota(n!)}, \qquad e:=\exp(1),$$
provided by the all-real convergence proved in [[lem-exponential-series-has-infinite-radius]]. Here $n!\in\mathbb N$ is the factorial of [[def-factorial-and-falling-factorial]], $\iota(n!)$ is its nonzero real image ([[def-canonical-natural]], [[lem-of-naturals-positive]]), and powers and series are those of [[def-integer-power]] and [[def-series]].

This is a real power series centred at $0$ ([[def-real-power-series-and-radius-of-convergence]]). No logarithm, irrational power, or differential equation enters the definition.

supplier_excerpts.exact_statement:
Let $a, b \in \mathbb{R}$ with $a < b$ and let $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be
continuous on $[a,b]$ ([[def-continuity-real]], [[def-interval]]) and
differentiable at every point of $(a,b)$ as a function on $[a,b]$
([[def-derivative]]). Then there is $c \in (a,b)$ with

$$f(b) - f(a) \;=\; f'(c)\,(b - a) .$$

Equivalently, since $b - a \ne 0$, there is $c \in (a,b)$ at which
$f'(c) = \bigl(f(b)-f(a)\bigr)/(b-a)$: the derivative somewhere inside equals
the average rate of change across the whole interval.

**Continuity on the closed interval cannot be dropped.** Differentiability at
every point of $(a,b)$ alone does not suffice: a function on $[0,1]$,
differentiable at every point of $(0,1)$ with derivative constantly $1$, for
which no $c$ works, is exhibited later on this page as a false statement, and
the companion page works the same witness out in full.

supplier_excerpts.exact_statement:
Let $A, B \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ with
$g[A] \subseteq B$ and let $f : B \to \mathbb{R}$, so that the composite
$f \circ g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ is defined. Let $c \in A$ be a limit point of
$A$ ([[def-limit-point-r]]) at which $g$ is differentiable
([[def-derivative]]), put $b := g(c)$, and suppose $b$ is a limit point of $B$
at which $f$ is differentiable. Then $f \circ g$ is differentiable at $c$ and

$$(f \circ g)'(c) \;=\; f'\bigl(g(c)\bigr)\,g'(c) .$$

**Both limit-point hypotheses are needed, and neither is automatic.** That $c$
is a limit point of $A$ is what makes $g'(c)$ and $(f \circ g)'(c)$ defined
symbols; that $b = g(c)$ is a limit point of $B$ is what makes $f'(b)$ one.
Nothing forces the second: $g$ may be differentiable at $c$ and send $c$ to an
isolated point of $B$, and there $f'(b)$ is not defined and the formula asserts
nothing.

**No case analysis appears anywhere.** The naive difference-quotient proof
writes $\frac{f(g(x)) - f(g(c))}{g(x) - g(c)} \cdot \frac{g(x) - g(c)}{x - c}$
and then has to say what happens where $g(x) = g(c)$, which may occur at points
arbitrarily close to $c$. Carathéodory's factorisation never divides by the
inner increment, so the difficulty does not arise.

supplier_excerpts.exact_statement:
Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $c \in A$ be a limit point of $A$
([[def-limit-point-r]]), let $f, g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ be differentiable at $c$
([[def-derivative]]) and let $\alpha \in \mathbb{R}$. Then:

1. $f + g$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(f+g)'(c) = f'(c) + g'(c)$;
2. $\alpha f$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(\alpha f)'(c) = \alpha f'(c)$;
3. $fg$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(fg)'(c) = f'(c)g(c) + f(c)g'(c)$;
4. if $g(c) \ne 0$ then, writing $A_0 := \{\, x \in A : g(x) \ne 0 \,\}$, the
   point $c$ lies in $A_0$ and is a limit point of $A_0$, the quotient
   $(f/g)|_{A_0} : A_0 \to \mathbb{R}$, $x \mapsto f(x)/g(x)$, is differentiable
   at $c$ as a function on $A_0$, and
   $$\bigl((f/g)|_{A_0}\bigr)'(c) \;=\; \frac{f'(c)\,g(c) - f(c)\,g'(c)}{g(c)^{2}} .$$

Each claim asserts two things: that the derivative on the left exists, and that
it has the stated value. Both are proved.

**Why claim 4 is stated on $A_0$.** The function $f/g$ is not defined where $g$
vanishes, and $g$ may vanish at points of $A$ far from $c$; restricting to $A_0$
is forced. That the restriction still has $c$ as a limit point, so that a
derivative there means anything at all, is not free either, and it is the last
claim of [[lem-sign-preservation-near-a-limit]] applied to $g$. The hypothesis
is $g(c) \ne 0$, not "$g$ vanishes nowhere".

**Everything is proved through
[[thm-caratheodory-characterisation]].** No difference quotient is estimated and
no limit theorem beyond continuity is used, so no choice principle is spent.
The four identities are four algebraic rearrangements of an increment, each
followed by a reading of [[thm-algebra-of-continuous-functions]].

Assume AC, fix $d\geq1$ and $\lambda>0$, and let $Q_\lambda$ be the configuration law of [[def-tdmath-poisson-configuration-reference]]. Define the intensity measure on Borel sets by $\Lambda_{Q_\lambda}(A):=E_{Q_\lambda}N_A$, where $N_A=\omega(A)$ and the nonnegative expectation may be infinite. For pairwise disjoint bounded Borel sets $A_1,\ldots,A_r\subseteq\mathbb R^d$, the restrictions $\omega|_{A_1},\ldots,\omega|_{A_r}$ are independent, each count $N_{A_j}$ has Poisson law with mean $\lambda|A_j|$, and the joint law of counts on any finite disjoint family is the product of those Poisson laws. In particular, $Q_\lambda$ is invariant under every translation $T_x$, and $\Lambda_{Q_\lambda}(A)=\lambda|A|$ for every Borel $A$. For every bounded Borel $A$ and real $a$, its count also has the exact exponential moment
$$E_{Q_\lambda}e^{aN_A}=\exp\!\left(\lambda|A|(e^a-1)\right).$$

Assume the Axiom of Choice and fix an integer dimension $d\geq1$. For $i\in\mathbb Z^d$, let $C_i=i+[0,1)^d$. These are left-closed, right-open cells. For every $x\in\mathbb R^d$, [[lem-integer-part]] supplies the unique integers $i_j$ with $i_j\le x_j<i_j+1$, so $x$ belongs to exactly one $C_i$. The cells are Borel products of closed/open ray intersections and have volume one by [[thm-lebesgue-measure-of-a-box-of-every-kind]], whose statement covers this face convention. A finite configuration in $C_i$ is a finite subset of distinct points. Encode it by its cardinality $n\in\mathbb N_0$ and its uniquely lexicographically increasing list of local coordinates $(x_1-i,\ldots,x_n-i)\in([0,1)^d)^n$. Pad the code after its first $n$ coordinates with the zero vector. For fixed $n$, the strictly increasing lists form a Borel subset of $([0,1]^d)^n$, since lexicographic strict order is a finite union of coordinate-equality and coordinate-inequality conditions. Thus all codes form a Borel subset of $\mathbb N_0\times([0,1]^d)^{\mathbb N}$. Each factor $[0,1]^d$ is Polish as a closed subspace of complete $\mathbb R^d$ with a countable dense rational grid; $\mathbb N_0$ with its discrete metric is Polish. By [[lem-tdmath-counts-generate-configuration-sigma]], its sigma-algebra is generated by the counts $N_B$ for Borel $B\subseteq C_i$.

derivations.claim: Let $W=a+[0,m)^d$ be any integer cube, with $a\in\mathbb Z^d$ and integer $m\geq1$. Translation invariance and [F1] give $D(P_W\Vert Q_W)\leq c|W|$. If $A$ is any bounded Borel set, choose one such cube $W$ containing it; by restriction monotonicity [F2], every $P\in\mathcal H_c$ satisfies $D(P_A\Vert Q_A)\leq C_A:=c|W|$.

For any probability density $h$ relative to a probability $Q$ with $D(hQ\Vert Q)\leq C$, and any $K>1$, $$\int_{\{h>K\}}h\,dQ\leq\frac{C+1/e}{\log K}.$$ Indeed, $-u\log u\leq1/e$ on $[0,1]$, while $h\log h\geq h\log K$ on $\{h>K\}$. Split the entropy integral at $h=1$ and combine these bounds. Thus, for each fixed cube $W$, the densities $dP_W/dQ_W$ with $P\in\mathcal H_c$ have $L^1(Q_W)$ norm one and are uniformly integrable.

Fix $W$. By [F3], the weak closure $K_W$ of these densities in real $L^1(Q_W)$ is weakly compact. It is Hausdorff by [F6]. Every $h\in K_W$ remains nonnegative and has integral one: testing against each indicator and against $1$ gives weakly closed conditions by [F6]. Also $D(hQ_W\Vert Q_W)\leq c|W|$, because [F2] expresses $D$ as the supremum of weakly continuous affine functions of $h$, with continuity given by [F6]. Hence all entropy sublevels used below are closed in their local weak topologies.

Index all integer cubes $W=a+[0,m)^d$ with $a\in\mathbb Z^d$ and integer $m\geq1$ by their countable set of pairs $(a,m)$, and form the product $K_*:=\prod_WK_W$. It is compact by [A2] and Hausdorff because each weak $L^1$ topology is Hausdorff by [F6]. Impose the following closed conditions on its tuples: whenever $W\subseteq V$, the $W$-marginal of $h_VQ_V$ equals $h_WQ_W$; and, for every real translation $x$ and bounded local measurable test $f$, the two marginals containing the supports of $f$ and $f\circ T_x$ satisfy $E_Pf=E_P(f\circ T_x)$. Each equality is closed because it tests weak convergence against bounded measurable functions on a containing cube, which are continuous by [F6]. The intersection $K_{\rm stat}$ of these closed conditions is compact.

A tuple in $K_{\rm stat}$ defines consistent finite-dimensional laws on the countable standard-Borel cell spaces: for a finite set of cells, choose any integer cube containing it and take that marginal. If two cubes contain the same finite set, a larger integer cube contains both; the imposed nested consistency makes their induced laws agree. By [F4] there is a unique law $P$ on $\Omega$ with those marginals. The imposed equalities make $P$ stationary, and each origin-anchored cube $[0,m)^d$ retains $D(P_{[0,m)^d}\Vert Q_{[0,m)^d})\leq c m^d$. Therefore [F1] gives $I(P)\leq c$. The extension map identifies $K_{\rm stat}$ with the set of laws having these local marginals and entropy constraints.

The same variational inequality controls particle-count tails uniformly. Fix bounded $A$, choose $W\supseteq A$ as in step 1.1, and let $K\geq0$, $a>0$, and $M\in\mathbb N$. The bounded local test $\phi_M=a\min(N_A\mathbf1_{\{N_A>K\}},M)$ in [F2] gives $$aE_P\min(N_A\mathbf1_{\{N_A>K\}},M)\leq C_A+\log E_Q\exp(\phi_M).$$ As $M\to\infty$, monotone convergence yields $$aE_P[N_A\mathbf1_{\{N_A>K\}}]\leq C_A+\log E_Qe^{aN_A\mathbf1_{\{N_A>K\}}}.$$ By [F5] and dominated convergence the logarithmic term tends to zero as $K\to\infty$. First choose $a$ large and then $K$ large; this proves uniform integrability of the counts $N_A$ over every law in the closure family, and in particular finite intensity for its limit laws.

The product compactness in step 3.1 first gives compactness for all bounded local tests. For any tame $f$ supported in $A$ with $|f|\leq b(1+N_A)$, set $f_K=f\mathbf1_{\{N_A\leq K\}}$. Then $f_K$ is bounded and local, and its expectation is weakly continuous by [F6], while $$\sup_{P\in\mathcal H_c}|E_P(f-f_K)|\leq b\sup_{P\in\mathcal H_c}E_P[(1+N_A)\mathbf1_{\{N_A>K\}}]\longrightarrow0$$ by step 5.1. Thus on the entropy level the tame expectation maps are uniform limits of bounded-local continuous maps. Every $P\in\mathcal H_c$ supplies its cube densities and gives a tuple in $K_{\rm stat}$, so the extension map from $K_{\rm stat}$ is onto; the local expectations just shown make it continuous. Its image $\mathcal H_c$ is compact in $\tau_L$.

Each $K_W$ is weakly compact in real $L^1(Q_W)$ and hence weakly sequentially compact by [F3]. Given a sequence in $K_{\rm stat}$, successively take subsequences converging in the first, second, and later cube coordinates and diagonalize; AC supplies the countable choices. The limit tuple preserves all closed consistency, stationarity, and entropy constraints from step 3.1, so it gives a law in $\mathcal H_c$ by step 4.1. Count-tail uniformity from step 5.1 upgrades coordinate convergence on bounded local tests to convergence for every tame test by the same truncation estimate in step 6.1. Hence $\mathcal H_c$ is sequentially compact in $\tau_L$.

citations.quote: A measure space is a triple $(X,\Sigma,\mu)$ where $\Sigma$ contains $\varnothing,X$ and is closed under complements and countable unions (a $\sigma$-algebra) of subsets of $X$ and $\mu:\Sigma\to[0,\infty]$ is countably additive with $\mu(\varnothing)=0$. A measurable function $f:X\to[-\infty,\infty]$ has measurable inverse images of Borel sets, where $[-\infty,\infty]$ has its order topology: finite open intervals and the endpoint neighborhoods $[-\infty,a)$ and $(a,\infty]$ form a basis. Its Borel sigma-algebra is generated by these open sets. A complex-valued function is measurable exactly when its finite real and imaginary parts are measurable, equivalently for the usual Borel structure of $\mathbb C$. Almost-everywhere assertions mean outside a measurable $\mu$-null set; completeness of $\mu$ is not assumed. Nonnegative extended addition uses $a+\infty=\infty+a=\infty$ for $a\in[0,\infty]$; positive scalars multiply $\infty$ to $\infty$, while $0\cdot\infty=0$. Signed expressions $\infty-\infty$ remain undefined and are not used in signed integrals. A nonnegative simple function has the form $s=\sum_{j=1}^m c_j\mathbf1_{A_j}$ with finitely many disjoint $A_j\in\Sigma$ and finite $c_j\ge0$. Define $c\mu(A)=+\infty$ if $c>0$ and $\mu(A)=+\infty$, define $0\cdot\infty:=0$, and define the finite sum of these extended nonnegative terms to be $+\infty$ if any term is $+\infty$ and otherwise the real finite sum of [[def-finite-sum]]. Then $\int s\,d\mu:=\sum_j c_j\mu(A_j)$; using canonical level sets $\{s=c\}$ makes this value representation-independent. For measurable $f\ge0$, define $\int f\,d\mu:=\sup\{\int s\,d\mu: s\text{ is simple and }0\le s\le f\}$, using [[def-complete-ordered-field]] for a bounded set of finite values and setting the supremum to $+\infty$ when the values are unbounded or one is infinite. A real measurable $f$ is integrable when $\int|f|\,d\mu<\infty$, and then $\int f:=\int f^+-\int f^-$, where $f^+=\max(f,0)$ and $f^-:=\max(-f,0)$. Complex integrability and integration are defined by integrable real and imaginary parts.

Let $(X,\Sigma,\mu)$ be a measure space and let $f_n:X\to\mathbb C$ be measurable with $f_n\to f$ almost everywhere. Suppose $g\ge0$ is measurable and $\int g\,d\mu<\infty$, and $|f_n|\le g$ almost everywhere for every $n$. Let $f_0(x)$ be the finite complex pointwise limit of $(f_n(x))$ where it exists, and $0$ elsewhere. Then $f_0$ is measurable, equals $f$ almost everywhere, is integrable, and $\int f_n\,d\mu\to\int f_0\,d\mu$ and $\int|f_n-f_0|\,d\mu\to0$. If the specified $f$ is measurable, these same conclusions hold with $f$ in place of $f_0$. In particular this is automatic when $\mu$ is complete. On a noncomplete measure space an arbitrary almost-everywhere representative need not be measurable, so no integral of such a nonmeasurable $f$ is asserted.

For $x\in\mathbb R$, define
$$\exp(x):=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\frac{x^n}{\iota(n!)}, \qquad e:=\exp(1),$$
provided by the all-real convergence proved in [[lem-exponential-series-has-infinite-radius]]. Here $n!\in\mathbb N$ is the factorial of [[def-factorial-and-falling-factorial]], $\iota(n!)$ is its nonzero real image ([[def-canonical-natural]], [[lem-of-naturals-positive]]), and powers and series are those of [[def-integer-power]] and [[def-series]].

This is a real power series centred at $0$ ([[def-real-power-series-and-radius-of-convergence]]). No logarithm, irrational power, or differential equation enters the definition.

The real exponential function is $C^\infty$, and for every $m\in\mathbb N$,
$$\exp^{(m)}=\exp.$$
In particular $(\exp)'=\exp$.

For $x>0$, define $\log x$ to be the unique real $y$ such that $\exp(y)=x$. This is well-defined because [[cor-exponential-is-a-bijection-onto-positive-reals]] states that $\exp:\mathbb R\to(0,\infty)$ is a bijection.

Thus $\log:(0,\infty)\to\mathbb R$ is the inverse function of $\exp$. In particular, $\log(\exp y)=y$ for every $y\in\mathbb R$ and $\exp(\log x)=x$ for every $x>0$.

The function $\log:(0,\infty)\to\mathbb R$ is continuous and strictly increasing, is onto $\mathbb R$, and satisfies, for $x,y>0$,
$$\log(xy)=\log x+\log y,\qquad \log(x/y)=\log x-\log y,\qquad \log(1/x)=-\log x.$$
Also $\log 1=0$.

For $x>0$, $\log$ is differentiable and
$$\log'(x)=\frac1x,\qquad \log x=\int_1^x\frac{dt}{t}.$$

Let $a, b \in \mathbb{R}$ with $a < b$ and let $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be
continuous on $[a,b]$ ([[def-continuity-real]], [[def-interval]]) and
differentiable at every point of $(a,b)$ as a function on $[a,b]$
([[def-derivative]]). Then there is $c \in (a,b)$ with

$$f(b) - f(a) \;=\; f'(c)\,(b - a) .$$

Equivalently, since $b - a \ne 0$, there is $c \in (a,b)$ at which
$f'(c) = \bigl(f(b)-f(a)\bigr)/(b-a)$: the derivative somewhere inside equals
the average rate of change across the whole interval.

**Continuity on the closed interval cannot be dropped.** Differentiability at
every point of $(a,b)$ alone does not suffice: a function on $[0,1]$,
differentiable at every point of $(0,1)$ with derivative constantly $1$, for
which no $c$ works, is exhibited later on this page as a false statement, and
the companion page works the same witness out in full.

Let $A, B \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ with
$g[A] \subseteq B$ and let $f : B \to \mathbb{R}$, so that the composite
$f \circ g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ is defined. Let $c \in A$ be a limit point of
$A$ ([[def-limit-point-r]]) at which $g$ is differentiable
([[def-derivative]]), put $b := g(c)$, and suppose $b$ is a limit point of $B$
at which $f$ is differentiable. Then $f \circ g$ is differentiable at $c$ and

$$(f \circ g)'(c) \;=\; f'\bigl(g(c)\bigr)\,g'(c) .$$

**Both limit-point hypotheses are needed, and neither is automatic.** That $c$
is a limit point of $A$ is what makes $g'(c)$ and $(f \circ g)'(c)$ defined
symbols; that $b = g(c)$ is a limit point of $B$ is what makes $f'(b)$ one.
Nothing forces the second: $g$ may be differentiable at $c$ and send $c$ to an
isolated point of $B$, and there $f'(b)$ is not defined and the formula asserts
nothing.

**No case analysis appears anywhere.** The naive difference-quotient proof
writes $\frac{f(g(x)) - f(g(c))}{g(x) - g(c)} \cdot \frac{g(x) - g(c)}{x - c}$
and then has to say what happens where $g(x) = g(c)$, which may occur at points
arbitrarily close to $c$. Carathéodory's factorisation never divides by the
inner increment, so the difficulty does not arise.

Let $(X,\mathcal{A})$, $(Y,\mathcal{B})$, and $(Z,\mathcal{C})$ be measurable
spaces. If $f : (X,\mathcal{A}) \to (Y,\mathcal{B})$ is measurable and
$g : (Y,\mathcal{B}) \to (Z,\mathcal{C})$ is measurable, then
$g \circ f : (X,\mathcal{A}) \to (Z,\mathcal{C})$ is measurable.

In particular, if $f$ is measurable and $g$ is a Borel measurable function on
its codomain, then $g \circ f$ is measurable.

derivations.claim: For each fixed parameter, measurable energy/observable coordinates and [F7] make every finite linear combination, exponential weight, weighted first/second moment and parameter difference quotient measurable; their displayed pointwise derivative limits are the same measurable compositions. For $\beta$ in the interior of a compact interval $K\subset J$, the difference quotient of $e^{-\beta E(x)}$ tends pointwise to $-E(x)e^{-\beta E(x)}$. The mean-value theorem [F5] bounds its absolute value, for small $h$, by $|E|e^{-\theta E}$ for an intermediate $\theta\in K$; this is at most $G_K$ because $|E|\le1+|E|^2$. Dominated convergence [F2] therefore gives $Z'=-\int E e^{-\beta E}d\mu$. Applying the same argument to $-E e^{-\beta E}$, dominated by $G_K$, gives $Z''=\int E^2e^{-\beta E}d\mu$; dominated convergence also gives continuity of both derivatives.

The density $p_\beta$ is nonnegative and integrates to one. The envelope makes its first and second energy moments finite. Differentiating $\log Z$ using [F4] gives $-Z'/Z=\int E p_\beta d\mu$ and $Z''/Z-(Z'/Z)^2=\int E^2p_\beta d\mu-(\int Ep_\beta d\mu)^2$. The latter is the variance by expanding its defining square.

Since $\log p_\beta=-\beta E-\log Z$ almost everywhere and $\int |E|p_\beta d\mu<\infty$, the entropy integrand is absolutely integrable. Substitution and normalization yield $-\int p_\beta\log p_\beta d\mu=\beta\langle E\rangle_\beta+\log Z$. This entropy depends on the chosen reference measure $\mu$.

supplier_excerpts.exact_statement: A measure space is a triple $(X,\Sigma,\mu)$ where $\Sigma$ contains $\varnothing,X$ and is closed under complements and countable unions (a $\sigma$-algebra) of subsets of $X$ and $\mu:\Sigma\to[0,\infty]$ is countably additive with $\mu(\varnothing)=0$. A measurable function $f:X\to[-\infty,\infty]$ has measurable inverse images of Borel sets, where the Borel sets of the extended real line are the sigma-algebra generated by its open sets. A nonnegative simple function has the form $s=\sum_{j=1}^m c_j\mathbf1_{A_j}$ with finitely many disjoint $A_j\in\Sigma$ and finite $c_j\ge0$. Define $c\mu(A)=+\infty$ if $c>0$ and $\mu(A)=+\infty$, define $0\cdot\infty:=0$, and define the finite sum of these extended nonnegative terms to be $+\infty$ if any term is $+\infty$ and otherwise the real finite sum of [[def-finite-sum]]. Then $\int s\,d\mu:=\sum_j c_j\mu(A_j)$; using canonical level sets $\{s=c\}$ makes this value representation-independent. For measurable $f\ge0$, define $\int f\,d\mu:=\sup\{\int s\,d\mu: s\text{ is simple and }0\le s\le f\}$, using [[def-complete-ordered-field]] for a bounded set of finite values and setting the supremum to $+\infty$ when the values are unbounded or one is infinite. A real measurable $f$ is integrable when $\int|f|\,d\mu<\infty$, and then $\int f:=\int f^+-\int f^-$, where $f^+=\max(f,0)$ and $f^-:=\max(-f,0)$. Complex integrability and integration are defined by integrable real and imaginary parts.

citations.quote: A measure space is a triple $(X,\Sigma,\mu)$ where $\Sigma$ contains $\varnothing,X$ and is closed under complements and countable unions (a $\sigma$-algebra) of subsets of $X$ and $\mu:\Sigma\to[0,\infty]$ is countably additive with $\mu(\varnothing)=0$. A measurable function $f:X\to[-\infty,\infty]$ has measurable inverse images of Borel sets, where $[-\infty,\infty]$ has its order topology: finite open intervals and the endpoint neighborhoods $[-\infty,a)$ and $(a,\infty]$ form a basis. Its Borel sigma-algebra is generated by these open sets. A complex-valued function is measurable exactly when its finite real and imaginary parts are measurable, equivalently for the usual Borel structure of $\mathbb C$. Almost-everywhere assertions mean outside a measurable $\mu$-null set; completeness of $\mu$ is not assumed. Nonnegative extended addition uses $a+\infty=\infty+a=\infty$ for $a\in[0,\infty]$; positive scalars multiply $\infty$ to $\infty$, while $0\cdot\infty=0$. Signed expressions $\infty-\infty$ remain undefined and are not used in signed integrals. A nonnegative simple function has the form $s=\sum_{j=1}^m c_j\mathbf1_{A_j}$ with finitely many disjoint $A_j\in\Sigma$ and finite $c_j\ge0$. Define $c\mu(A)=+\infty$ if $c>0$ and $\mu(A)=+\infty$, define $0\cdot\infty:=0$, and define the finite sum of these extended nonnegative terms to be $+\infty$ if any term is $+\infty$ and otherwise the real finite sum of [[def-finite-sum]]. Then $\int s\,d\mu:=\sum_j c_j\mu(A_j)$; using canonical level sets $\{s=c\}$ makes this value representation-independent. For measurable $f\ge0$, define $\int f\,d\mu:=\sup\{\int s\,d\mu: s\text{ is simple and }0\le s\le f\}$, using [[def-complete-ordered-field]] for a bounded set of finite values and setting the supremum to $+\infty$ when the values are unbounded or one is infinite. A real measurable $f$ is integrable when $\int|f|\,d\mu<\infty$, and then $\int f:=\int f^+-\int f^-$, where $f^+=\max(f,0)$ and $f^-:=\max(-f,0)$. Complex integrability and integration are defined by integrable real and imaginary parts.

Throughout this page $\mathbb{R}$ is the complete ordered field
([[def-complete-ordered-field]]), in particular an ordered field
([[def-ordered-field]]) and a field ([[def-field]]), and $\mathbb{N}$ is the set
of natural numbers ([[def-natural-numbers]]) with successor $\sigma(n) = n + 1$
([[def-nat-addition]]).

Let $a : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{R}$ be a sequence of reals, written $a_k$ for
$a(k)$. **Finite sums and finite products of $a$ are defined by recursion on the
upper index**, which is legitimate because of the recursion theorem
([[thm-recursion]]). That theorem produces a function of one variable, so the
running index has to be carried along inside the value: applying it to the set
$A = \mathbb{N} \times \mathbb{R}$, the starting element $(0, 0)$ and the function
$f(n, s) = (\sigma(n),\, s + a_n)$ gives a unique
$g : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N} \times \mathbb{R}$ with

$$g(0) = (0, 0), \qquad g(\sigma(n)) = f(g(n)) \quad (n \in \mathbb{N}).$$

Write $g(n) = \big(\pi_1(g(n)),\, \Sigma_n\big)$ for its two coordinates.

**The first coordinate is the index itself, and that is a small induction, not an
observation** ([[thm-induction-principle]]). Indeed $\pi_1(g(0)) = 0$; and if
$\pi_1(g(n)) = n$, then
$g(\sigma(n)) = f\big(\pi_1(g(n)), \Sigma_n\big) = \big(\sigma(\pi_1(g(n))),\, \Sigma_n + a_{\pi_1(g(n))}\big) = \big(\sigma(n),\, \Sigma_n + a_n\big)$,
so $\pi_1(g(\sigma(n))) = \sigma(n)$. By induction $\pi_1(g(n)) = n$ for every
$n \in \mathbb{N}$. Only now may the second coordinate of the two displayed
clauses be read off, and doing so gives

$$\Sigma_0 = 0, \qquad \Sigma_{\sigma(n)} = \Sigma_n + a_n .$$

$\Sigma$ is moreover the **unique** function $\mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{R}$ with those
two properties: if $\Sigma'$ also has them then $n \mapsto (n, \Sigma'_n)$ satisfies
the two clauses defining $g$, hence equals $g$ by the uniqueness clause of
[[thm-recursion]], so $\Sigma' = \Sigma$.

We write $\sum_{k < n} a_k := \Sigma_n$. The same construction with starting
element $(0, 1)$ and $f(n, p) = (\sigma(n),\, p \cdot a_n)$, with the same
induction on the first coordinate and the same uniqueness argument, gives the
unique $\Pi : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{R}$ with

and we write $\prod_{k < n} a_k := \Pi_n$.

$$\sum_{k=0}^{n} a_k := \sum_{k < n+1} a_k, \qquad \prod_{k=0}^{n} a_k := \prod_{k < n+1} a_k,$$

and, for a general lower index $m$ with $m \le n + 1$, writing $d = n + 1 - m$
for the number of terms,

$$\sum_{k=m}^{n} a_k := \sum_{j < d} a_{m+j}, \qquad \prod_{k=m}^{n} a_k := \prod_{j < d} a_{m+j} .$$

When $m = n + 1$ we have $d = 0$ and the sum is **empty**, with value $0$, while
the empty product has value $1$. In the same spirit $\sum_{k=0}^{-1} a_k$ is
notation for the empty sum $\Sigma_0 = 0$ and $\prod_{k=0}^{-1} a_k$ for the

$a_0, \dots, a_{n-1}$ of reals given without reference to any extension of the
list to all of $\mathbb{N}$: extend the list by $a_k = 0$ (respectively
$a_k = 1$) for $k \ge n$ and apply the definition above.

Let $F$ be an ordered field ([[def-ordered-field]]) and $S \subseteq F$.

- $u \in F$ is an **upper bound** of $S$ if $s \le u$ for all $s \in S$; $S$ is
  **bounded above** if it has an upper bound.
- $u \in F$ is a **least upper bound** (or **supremum**, $\sup S$) of $S$ if $u$
  is an upper bound of $S$ and $u \le u'$ for every upper bound $u'$ of $S$.

$F$ is a **complete ordered field** (equivalently, $F$ has the
**least-upper-bound property**, or is **Dedekind complete**) if every nonempty

derivations.claim: For every finite real $a$, $\{f>a\}=\bigcup_n\{f_n>a\}$, since the sequence increases to $f$. These threshold sets generate the order-topology Borel sigma-algebra in [F1], so $f$ is measurable. The simple minorants of $f_n$ are also minorants of $f_{n+1}$, so their integral suprema increase. Each is at most $\int f$; hence $L:=\lim_n\int f_n$ exists in $[0,\infty]$ and $L\le\int f$.

Fix a nonnegative simple $s\le f$ and $0<t<1$. The measurable sets $A_n:=\{f_n\ge ts\}$ increase and cover $\{s>0\}$, since $f_n(x)\to f(x)\ge s(x)>ts(x)$ there. Write $s=\sum_{j=1}^m c_j\mathbf1_{B_j}$ in disjoint level form. For each $c_j>0$, $A_n\cap B_j\uparrow B_j$; countable additivity, applied to successive disjoint differences, gives $\mu(A_n\cap B_j)\uparrow\mu(B_j)$. The finite-sum definition [F2] then gives $\int s\mathbf1_{A_n}\uparrow\int s$. As $f_n\ge ts\mathbf1_{A_n}$, monotonicity and homogeneity of the simple integral imply $L\ge t\int s$. Let $t\uparrow1$ and take the supremum over $s\le f$; [F1, F3] give $L\ge\int f$. Together with step 1.1 this proves monotone convergence.

For nonnegative measurable $f$, define $s_n:=2^{-n}\sum_{k=1}^{n2^n}\mathbf1_{\{f\ge k2^{-n}\}}$. Each $s_n$ is a finite-valued measurable simple function. Every threshold counted in $s_n$ is also counted at the even-index threshold in $s_{n+1}$, so $s_n\le s_{n+1}$. If $f(x)<\infty$, once $n>f(x)$ the mesh gives $0\le f(x)-s_n(x)<2^{-n}$; if $f(x)=\infty$, then $s_n(x)=n$. Thus $s_n\uparrow f$. Define $t_n:=2^{-n}\sum_{k=1}^{n2^n}\mathbf1_{\{g\ge k2^{-n}\}}$; the same threshold and mesh argument shows $t_n\uparrow g$. By [F4], $f+g$ and $s_n+t_n$ are measurable with the defined nonnegative extended addition. Apply the monotone-convergence conclusion of step 2.1 to $s_n$, $t_n$, and $s_n+t_n$. Refine their finitely many level sets to the finite partition of intersections $B_j\cap C_k$; regrouping the resulting sums by [F2] gives $\int(s_n+t_n)=\int s_n+\int t_n$. Passing to the three monotone limits proves $\int(f+g)=\int f+\int g$.

For $c>0$, simple minorants of $cf$ are exactly $c$ times simple minorants of $f$, so the supremum definition gives $\int cf=c\int f$; for $c=0$ both sides are zero. If an integrable real function is expressed as $u-v$ with $u,v\ge0$ integrable, the value $\int u-\int v$ is independent of the expression: $u-v=u'-v'$ implies $u+v'=u'+v$, and step 2.2 equates the finite sums of integrals. The definition using positive and negative parts is one such expression, so signed integrals are linear.

supplier_excerpts.exact_statement: A measure space is a triple $(X,\Sigma,\mu)$ where $\Sigma$ contains $\varnothing,X$ and is closed under complements and countable unions (a $\sigma$-algebra) of subsets of $X$ and $\mu:\Sigma\to[0,\infty]$ is countably additive with $\mu(\varnothing)=0$. A measurable function $f:X\to[-\infty,\infty]$ has measurable inverse images of Borel sets, where the Borel sets of the extended real line are the sigma-algebra generated by its open sets. A nonnegative simple function has the form $s=\sum_{j=1}^m c_j\mathbf1_{A_j}$ with finitely many disjoint $A_j\in\Sigma$ and finite $c_j\ge0$. Define $c\mu(A)=+\infty$ if $c>0$ and $\mu(A)=+\infty$, define $0\cdot\infty:=0$, and define the finite sum of these extended nonnegative terms to be $+\infty$ if any term is $+\infty$ and otherwise the real finite sum of [[def-finite-sum]]. Then $\int s\,d\mu:=\sum_j c_j\mu(A_j)$; using canonical level sets $\{s=c\}$ makes this value representation-independent. For measurable $f\ge0$, define $\int f\,d\mu:=\sup\{\int s\,d\mu: s\text{ is simple and }0\le s\le f\}$, using [[def-complete-ordered-field]] for a bounded set of finite values and setting the supremum to $+\infty$ when the values are unbounded or one is infinite. A real measurable $f$ is integrable when $\int|f|\,d\mu<\infty$, and then $\int f:=\int f^+-\int f^-$, where $f^+=\max(f,0)$ and $f^-:=\max(-f,0)$. Complex integrability and integration are defined by integrable real and imaginary parts.

Throughout this page $\mathbb{R}$ is the complete ordered field
([[def-complete-ordered-field]]), in particular an ordered field
([[def-ordered-field]]) and a field ([[def-field]]), and $\mathbb{N}$ is the set
of natural numbers ([[def-natural-numbers]]) with successor $\sigma(n) = n + 1$
([[def-nat-addition]]).

Let $a : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{R}$ be a sequence of reals, written $a_k$ for
$a(k)$. **Finite sums and finite products of $a$ are defined by recursion on the
upper index**, which is legitimate because of the recursion theorem
([[thm-recursion]]). That theorem produces a function of one variable, so the
running index has to be carried along inside the value: applying it to the set
$A = \mathbb{N} \times \mathbb{R}$, the starting element $(0, 0)$ and the function
$f(n, s) = (\sigma(n),\, s + a_n)$ gives a unique
$g : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N} \times \mathbb{R}$ with

$$g(0) = (0, 0), \qquad g(\sigma(n)) = f(g(n)) \quad (n \in \mathbb{N}).$$

Write $g(n) = \big(\pi_1(g(n)),\, \Sigma_n\big)$ for its two coordinates.

**The first coordinate is the index itself, and that is a small induction, not an
observation** ([[thm-induction-principle]]). Indeed $\pi_1(g(0)) = 0$; and if
$\pi_1(g(n)) = n$, then
$g(\sigma(n)) = f\big(\pi_1(g(n)), \Sigma_n\big) = \big(\sigma(\pi_1(g(n))),\, \Sigma_n + a_{\pi_1(g(n))}\big) = \big(\sigma(n),\, \Sigma_n + a_n\big)$,
so $\pi_1(g(\sigma(n))) = \sigma(n)$. By induction $\pi_1(g(n)) = n$ for every
$n \in \mathbb{N}$. Only now may the second coordinate of the two displayed
clauses be read off, and doing so gives

$$\Sigma_0 = 0, \qquad \Sigma_{\sigma(n)} = \Sigma_n + a_n .$$

$\Sigma$ is moreover the **unique** function $\mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{R}$ with those
two properties: if $\Sigma'$ also has them then $n \mapsto (n, \Sigma'_n)$ satisfies
the two clauses defining $g$, hence equals $g$ by the uniqueness clause of
[[thm-recursion]], so $\Sigma' = \Sigma$.

We write $\sum_{k < n} a_k := \Sigma_n$. The same construction with starting
element $(0, 1)$ and $f(n, p) = (\sigma(n),\, p \cdot a_n)$, with the same
induction on the first coordinate and the same uniqueness argument, gives the
unique $\Pi : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{R}$ with

$$\Pi_0 = 1, \qquad \Pi_{\sigma(n)} = \Pi_n \cdot a_n ,$$

and we write $\prod_{k < n} a_k := \Pi_n$.

**Notation.** For $m, n \in \mathbb{N}$ we abbreviate

$$\sum_{k=0}^{n} a_k := \sum_{k < n+1} a_k, \qquad \prod_{k=0}^{n} a_k := \prod_{k < n+1} a_k,$$

and, for a general lower index $m$ with $m \le n + 1$, writing $d = n + 1 - m$
for the number of terms,

$$\sum_{k=m}^{n} a_k := \sum_{j < d} a_{m+j}, \qquad \prod_{k=m}^{n} a_k := \prod_{j < d} a_{m+j} .$$

When $m = n + 1$ we have $d = 0$ and the sum is **empty**, with value $0$, while
the empty product has value $1$. In the same spirit $\sum_{k=0}^{-1} a_k$ is
notation for the empty sum $\Sigma_0 = 0$ and $\prod_{k=0}^{-1} a_k$ for the
empty product $\Pi_0 = 1$; the index $-1$ never occurs as an element of
$\mathbb{N}$ and is only a way of writing "no terms".

Only finitely many values of $a$ enter $\sum_{k<n} a_k$, so the notation
$\sum_{k<n} a_k$ and $\prod_{k<n} a_k$ is also used for a list
$a_0, \dots, a_{n-1}$ of reals given without reference to any extension of the
list to all of $\mathbb{N}$: extend the list by $a_k = 0$ (respectively
$a_k = 1$) for $k \ge n$ and apply the definition above.

citations.quote: The far image sum is absolutely convergent for all sufficiently large $L$ by [[lem-tdmath-integrable-tail-diagonal-gap]]; this is the image convention used below.
The tail of the cell envelope $\psi(|j|_\infty-1)$ over all sufficiently large integer offsets is summable.

For the unit cells $C_i=i+[0,1)^d$, there are constants $A>0$ and $B\geq0$ such that every finite configuration satisfies
$$H_\phi(\omega)\geq A\sum_{i\in\mathbb Z^d}N_{C_i}(\omega)^2-BN(\omega).$$
Only finitely many summands are nonzero.

For every $\rho>0$ in that interior and every such sequence $(L_j,N_j)$,
$$\lim_{j\to\infty}L_j^{-d}\log Z(L_j,N_j;\beta)=F(\rho).$$
No claim is made at a close-packing endpoint or at any other excluded endpoint.
Let $F_\beta$ be the finite concave canonical rate on the interior attainable-density interval from [[thm-tdmath-canonical-interior-density-limit]].

For free and periodic cubes define
$$Z_{L,z,\beta,bc}=E_{Q_{\Lambda_L}}\!\left[z^{N_{\Lambda_L}}e^{-\beta H_{L,bc}}\right],\qquad bc\in\{\mathrm{free},\mathrm{per}\}.$$
Then the limit $p_Q(z,\beta)=\lim_{L\to\infty}L^{-d}\log Z_{L,z,\beta,bc}$ exists, is independent of $bc$, and
$$p_Q(z,\beta)=-\min_{P\in\mathcal P^1_{\rm stat}}\{I(P)+\beta\Phi(P)-\rho(P)\log z\}.$$
The minimizer set is nonempty and compact in the local-tame topology $\tau_L$.

Let $\Lambda_L=[0,L)^d$, $\beta,z>0$, and $b\in\{\mathrm{free},\mathrm{per}\}$. On the simple labelled sector $\mathcal S_{L,N}=\{q\in\Lambda_L^N:q_i\neq q_j\ (i\neq j)\}$ use $H_{L,\mathrm{free}}(q)=\sum_{i<j}\phi(q_i-q_j)$ and the periodic energy $H_{L,\mathrm{per}}$ from [[def-tdmath-superstable-regular-interaction]]. For $N\geq1$ define
$$Z_b(L,N;\beta)=\frac1{N!}\int_{\mathcal S_{L,N}}e^{-\beta H_{L,b}(q)}\,dq_1\cdots dq_N,\qquad Z_b(L,0;\beta)=1,$$
with $e^{-\beta(+\infty)}=0$, and put $\Xi_b(L,z,\beta)=\sum_{N\geq0}z^NZ_b(L,N;\beta)$. The unit-intensity Poisson reference $Q_{\Lambda_L}$ has sector density $e^{-L^d}/N!$ relative to labelled Lebesgue measure, so its normalized grand partition is
$$Z_{Q,b}(L;z,\beta)=E_{Q_{\Lambda_L}}[z^{N_{\Lambda_L}}e^{-\beta H_{L,b}}]=e^{-L^d}\Xi_b(L,z,\beta).$$
The exact-$N$ canonical law $C^b_{L,N}$ has density $e^{-\beta H_{L,b}}/(N!Z_b(L,N;\beta))$ on $\mathcal S_{L,N}$, and the grand-canonical law $G^b_{L,z,\beta}$ has density $z^{N_{\Lambda_L}}e^{-\beta H_{L,b}}/Z_{Q,b}(L;z,\beta)$ relative to $Q_{\Lambda_L}$. Let $\rho>0$ be an interior attainable density, choose $\alpha=\log z$ supporting the free canonical rate $F_\beta$ at $\rho$, and take $N_L/L^d\to\rho$. Assume
$$L^{-d}\log Z_b(L,N_L;\beta)\longrightarrow F_\beta(\rho).$$
Let $R_{L,\omega}$ be the periodized empirical field of [[def-tdmath-periodized-empirical-field]], and let
$$\mathcal M_{z,\beta}:=\operatorname*{argmin}_{P\in\mathcal P^1_{\rm stat}}\{I(P)+\beta\Phi(P)-\rho(P)\log z\}.$$
Then for every open $\tau_L$ neighborhood $U$ of $\mathcal M_{z,\beta}$ there is $c_U>0$ such that
$$\limsup_{L\to\infty}L^{-d}\log C^b_{L,N_L}\{\,\omega:R_{L,\omega}\notin U\,\}\leq-c_U.$$
If $\mathcal M_{z,\beta}=\{P_*\}$, then $R_{L,\omega}\to P_*$ in probability in $\tau_L$ under $C^b_{L,N_L}$. This is a statement about spatially averaged local observables through the empirical field, not about the raw finite-box law at a fixed origin.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a measure space, let $p,q\in[1,\infty]$ be
conjugate exponents, and let $f,g$ be measurable real-valued functions.

Define its **periodized empirical field**
$$R_{L,\omega}:=\frac1{L^d}\int_{\Lambda_L}\delta_{T_x\omega^{(L)}}\,dx.$$
The integral is the push-forward of normalized Lebesgue measure on $\Lambda_L$ under $x\mapsto T_x\omega^{(L)}$.

For $L>0$ and a finite configuration $\omega\subset\Lambda_L$ with $N(\omega)=N$, the measure $R_{L,\omega}$ of [[def-tdmath-periodized-empirical-field]] is a stationary probability law of finite intensity and
$$\rho(R_{L,\omega})=\frac{N}{L^d}.$$
For any probability law $C_L$ on finite configurations in $\Lambda_L$ with $E_{C_L}N<\infty$, its empirical-field barycenter $\bar C_L$ is also a stationary probability law of finite intensity and $\rho(\bar C_L)=E_{C_L}N/L^d$.

derivations.claim: For the upper bound, $e^{\alpha N_L}Z_{\mathrm{per}}(L,N_L;\beta)\leq\Xi_{\mathrm{per}}(L,e^\alpha,\beta)$ for every real $\alpha$. Divide logarithms by $L^d$, use the free/periodic grand limit [F6], and then take the infimum over $\alpha$. The canonical-grand duality [F5] gives $\limsup L^{-d}\log Z_{\mathrm{per}}\leq F_\beta(\rho)$.

Fix corridor width $k$ larger than the tail cutoff. Restrict the $N_L$ particles to the inner cube of side $L-k$, leaving the corridor empty. The exact-$N_L$ density is still $\rho$. The diagonal-gap supplier [F2] gives the vanishing regular-tail cutoff used here. By [L1], the periodized energy differs from the free inner-cube energy by at most $c_d\delta_kT_{L-k}$. The cell bound [F3] implies $T_{L-k}\leq A^{-1}(H_{L-k}+BN_L)$. Consequently $$ Z_{\mathrm{per}}(L,N_L;\beta)\geq e^{-\beta c_d\delta_k BN_L/A}\, Z(L-k,N_L;\beta(1+c_d\delta_k/A)). $$ The canonical theorem [F4] applies at the perturbed inverse temperature, giving the corresponding lower rate.

At fixed interior $\rho$, $F_\beta(\rho)$ is finite and convex as a function of $\beta>0$, by Hölder’s inequality [F8], since each finite-volume log partition is convex and the pointwise limit is finite. A finite convex function is continuous on the open interval: on a compact subinterval, its secant slopes are bounded by the slopes to fixed exterior endpoints. Let $L\to\infty$ in step 1.2 and then $k\to\infty$, so $\delta_k\to0$; continuity yields $\liminf\geq F_\beta(\rho)$.

Step 2.1 established the periodic exact-$N_L$ rate $F_\beta(\rho)$, and [F5] supplies a finite supporting activity. The grand rate in [F6] and the periodized empirical field in [F9] satisfy the hypotheses of [F7] with periodic boundary condition. Hence the periodic empirical fields concentrate near the minimizer set, and concentrate at its singleton when it is unique.

For integers $N_L$ with $N_L/L^d\to\rho$, let $Z_{\mathrm{per}}(L,N_L;\beta)$ be the $1/N_L!$-normalized positional partition on the periodized cube, with the image convention of [[def-tdmath-superstable-regular-interaction]]. Then
$$L^{-d}\log Z_{\mathrm{per}}(L,N_L;\beta)\longrightarrow F_\beta(\rho),$$

Let $C^{\mathrm{per}}_{L,N_L}$ be the periodic exact-$N_L$ canonical law and $R_{L,\omega}$ its periodized empirical field from [[def-tdmath-periodized-empirical-field]]. For any finite supporting activity $z>0$ of $F_\beta$ at $\rho$, these empirical fields concentrate in every open $\tau_L$ neighborhood of the minimizer set of $I+\beta\Phi-\rho\log z$. A singleton minimizer gives convergence in probability in $\tau_L$.

Assume the superstable regular interaction of [[thm-tdmath-continuum-variational-pressure]], $\beta>0$, and an interior attainable density $\rho>0$. For integers $N_L$ with $N_L/L^d\to\rho$, let $Z_{\mathrm{per}}(L,N_L;\beta)$ be the $1/N_L!$-normalized positional partition on the periodized cube, with the image convention of [[def-tdmath-superstable-regular-interaction]]. Then
$$L^{-d}\log Z_{\mathrm{per}}(L,N_L;\beta)\longrightarrow F_\beta(\rho),$$
the same rate as the free cube. Let $C^{\mathrm{per}}_{L,N_L}$ be the periodic exact-$N_L$ canonical law and $R_{L,\omega}$ its periodized empirical field from [[def-tdmath-periodized-empirical-field]]. For any finite supporting activity $z>0$ of $F_\beta$ at $\rho$, these empirical fields concentrate in every open $\tau_L$ neighborhood of the minimizer set of $I+\beta\Phi-\rho\log z$. A singleton minimizer gives convergence in probability in $\tau_L$.
