Let $P$ be a set of primitive type labels. A formal type $\Gamma$ records a finitely supported amount function $\nu_\Gamma:P\to\mathbb R_{\ge0}$, not identically zero. Primitive generators have their unit amount function. Positive scaling, separated product, and thermal-join constructors retain distinct formal tags and obey

$$\nu_{s\Gamma}=s\nu_\Gamma,\qquad \nu_{\Gamma\otimes\Gamma'}=\nu_\Gamma+\nu_{\Gamma'}\qquad(s>0).$$

Separated and joined types are distinct constructors even when their amount functions agree. Permutation, reassociation, and scaled-splitting conventions preserve the amount function. Define the positive **bookkeeping weight** $w_\Gamma:=\sum_{p\in P}\nu_\Gamma(p)$, a finite sum over support. Thus $w_{s\Gamma}=s w_\Gamma$ and every product or join has weight $w_\Gamma+w_{\Gamma'}$. The optional empty unit has zero amount function and weight zero; it is represented only by the empty compound, not as a simple chart. These are formal amounts, not masses in kilograms or an empirical conservation law. The functions and pointwise operations use [[def-function-space]]; their finite-support convention and finite sums are those of [[def-tdmath-tagged-scalable-compound]] and [[lem-tdmath-compound-mass-well-defined]].

Let $I$ index the declared family of simple types $\Gamma_i$. For each simple type $\Gamma$ in that family, let $n_\Gamma\ge1$ and let $\Gamma\subset\mathbb R^{n_\Gamma+1}$ be nonempty, open and convex, with coordinates $x=(u,v)$. The notation for a type and its chart is shared, but each state has a distinct raw tag $(\Gamma,x)$. Scaled charts are distinct tagged copies $s\Gamma=\{sx:x\in\Gamma\}$ with coordinate transport $x\mapsto sx$; transported raw tags remain distinct from the original raw tags. Let $e_{(\Gamma,x)}$ be the unit point mass from [[def-tdmath-tagged-scalable-compound]]. The represented state is

$$\mathsf{J}_\Gamma(x):=w_\Gamma e_{(\Gamma,x)},\qquad m(\mathsf{J}_\Gamma(x))=w_\Gamma.$$

Write $\mathsf{J}(x):=\mathsf{J}_\Gamma(x)$ when $x$ already carries its type tag. All state notation in this framework's compound comparisons, including a bare $x$, denotes $\mathsf{J}_\Gamma(x)$; a raw unit point mass is always written $e_{(\Gamma,x)}$. A separated pair is addition of represented states, not a unit product tag. Nonnegative multiples are pointwise and zero terms are omitted. For an encoded compound $c$, its aggregate composition is the finite amount function

$$\nu(c):=\sum_{(\Gamma,x)\in\operatorname{supp}(c)}\frac{c(\Gamma,x)}{w_\Gamma}\nu_\Gamma;\qquad m(c)=\sum_{p\in P}\nu(c)(p).$$

Fix the formal interpretation $\Pi(c)$ as the finite separated preparation whose factor at each nonzero raw tag $(\Gamma,x)$ is the amount $c(\Gamma,x)/w_\Gamma$ of that typed state, using the declared coordinate scaling transport. The accessibility relation on coefficient maps is the pullback of the declared relation on these preparations. Merging or splitting repeated copies of the same preparation is reversible; permutation and reassociation preserve the preparation. Thus $\Pi(\mathsf{J}_{s\Gamma}(sx))$ and $\Pi(s\mathsf{J}_\Gamma(x))$ are the same declared scaled preparation and yield

$$\mathsf{J}_{s\Gamma}(sx)\sim s\mathsf{J}_\Gamma(x),$$

although their raw point masses have different tags and are not equal. This reversible transport commutes with finite composition, nested type constructors, and scaled splitting. It is part of the precise formal scaling interpretation, not a deduction about physical accessibility from coordinate multiplication. A physical use must adopt the stated preparation maps and accessibility assumptions; fixed-composition models compare only preparations with the same $\nu$, while a declared channel model may additionally compare different compositions of equal $m$.

A comparison $A\prec B$ is defined only when $m(A)=m(B)$, as in the coefficient-map supplier. Write $A\sim B$ when both directions hold, and $A\prec\prec B$ when only the forward direction holds. On any fixed simple type, dividing every represented state by the same positive constant $w_\Gamma$ gives its unit-point-mass comparison. Positive scaling and its inverse preserve and reflect order; whenever the required CH and reference hypotheses hold, the unit-state entropy theorem applies after that normalization. If $S$ represents unit-point-mass comparisons, the entropy of a represented state is $w_\Gamma S(x)$ and the entropy of a finite sum $\sum_j t_j\mathsf{J}_\Gamma(x_j)$ is $\sum_j t_j w_\Gamma S(x_j)$. No independent rescaling across different types is assumed without a calibrator.

The common relation satisfies A1–A6 on all equal-mass finite compounds: (A1) reflexivity; (A2) transitivity; (A3) if $A\prec B$, then $A+C\prec B+C$ for every compound $C$; (A4) if $A\prec B$, then $tA\prec tB$ for every $t>0$; (A5) $t\mathsf{J}_\Gamma(x)$ is equivalent to $s\mathsf{J}_\Gamma(x)+(t-s)\mathsf{J}_\Gamma(x)$ for $t>0$ and $0<s<t$, with the reversible scaled-copy transport above; (A6) for equal-mass $A,B$, fixed positive equal-mass spectators $Z_0,Z_1$, and every sequence $\epsilon_n>0$ decreasing to zero, $A+\epsilon_n Z_0\prec B+\epsilon_n Z_1$ for all $n$ implies $A\prec B$. These are hypotheses, not conclusions. No comparison hypothesis is included here.

For each $i$ and $x\in\Gamma_i$, define the forward sector $A_x:=\{y\in\Gamma_i:\mathsf{J}_{\Gamma_i}(x)\prec\mathsf{J}_{\Gamma_i}(y)\}$. The simple-domain assumptions are: (A7) for $x,y\in\Gamma_i$ and $0<t<1$, the encoded compound $t\mathsf{J}_{\Gamma_i}(x)+(1-t)\mathsf{J}_{\Gamma_i}(y)$ compares to $\mathsf{J}_{\Gamma_i}(tx+(1-t)y)$; both have bookkeeping mass $w_{\Gamma_i}$, and convexity puts the recombined coordinate in the chart; (S1) each $x$ has a strict successor; (S2) $A_x$ has exactly one supporting hyperplane at $x$, expressible as $u-u_x+P_i(x)\cdot(v-v_x)=0$ with a finite-valued slope map $P_i:\Gamma_i\to\mathbb R^{n_i}$, and $P_i$ is locally Lipschitz; (S3) the boundary of $A_x$ relative to $\Gamma_i$ is arcwise connected. A supporting hyperplane means that $A_x$ lies in one of its closed half-spaces and meets the plane at $x$. The affine hull is the smallest affine subspace containing a set; relative interior is interior in that affine hull. Closure and boundary are taken in the indicated affine hull or in $\Gamma_i$, as named; boundary is closure intersected with closure of the complement in that relative topology.

This definition imposes no physical interpretation, units, or empirical claim. A contact theorem that uses joins must separately assume that each join is a simple domain satisfying these same forward-sector hypotheses.

For two simple domains $\Gamma_i\subset\mathbb R^{n_i+1}$ and $\Gamma_j\subset\mathbb R^{n_j+1}$, write their coordinates $(u_i,v_i)$ and $(u_j,v_j)$. Their thermal-join domain is

$$\Delta_{ij}:=\{(u,v_i,v_j):\exists u_i,u_j,\ (u_i,v_i)\in\Gamma_i,\ (u_j,v_j)\in\Gamma_j,\ u=u_i+u_j\}.$$

The joined simple type is a distinct formal tag with amount function $\nu_{\Delta_{ij}}=\nu_{\Gamma_i}+\nu_{\Gamma_j}$ and weight $w_{\Delta_{ij}}=w_{\Gamma_i}+w_{\Gamma_j}$, as defined in [[def-tdmath-forward-sector-hypotheses]]. Encode the separated pair by $\mathsf{J}_{\Gamma_i}(x)+\mathsf{J}_{\Gamma_j}(y)$ and a joined coordinate $Z$ by $\mathsf{J}_{\Delta_{ij}}(Z)$. Their bookkeeping masses agree, and their aggregate composition functions agree. These encoded maps and their raw tags remain distinct. Positive coordinate-scaled copies use the reversible preparation transport of that definition; nested joins preserve their finite primitive amount function under reassociation and permutation. The empty type contributes the zero map.

Write $J_{ij}(x,y)$ for the join state with the summed energy coordinate and the unchanged work coordinates. A compound pair $(x,y)$ and $J_{ij}(x,y)$ have the same total energy and work coordinates but are distinct tagged objects. Define $x\sim_T y$ exactly when $\mathsf{J}_{\Gamma_i}(x)+\mathsf{J}_{\Gamma_j}(y)$ and $\mathsf{J}_{\Delta_{ij}}(J_{ij}(x,y))$ are accessible in both directions. Nested joins use the declared reassociation and permutation identifications.

Assume every finite join is itself a simple domain satisfying [[def-tdmath-forward-sector-hypotheses]]. The contact hypotheses are mathematical assumptions on the common relation: (T1) $(x,y)\prec J_{ij}(x,y)$; (T2) every join state has at least one reversible split into component states at its stated coordinates, and the equal-state split of any state into positive scaled copies of itself is reversible; (T3) $\sim_T$ is transitive; (T4) for every simple state $x$ there are states $x_0,x_1$ in its domain with $x_0\prec\prec x\prec\prec x_1$ and $x_0\sim_T x_1$; (T5) for every ordered pair of simple systems, every $x$ in the first and every work coordinate $v$ in the second's projection $\rho(\Gamma_j):=\{v:\exists u,(u,v)\in\Gamma_j\}$, there is a state $y$ with work coordinate $v$ and $x\sim_T y$.

For the completed calibrator branch, add (C1) **join coherence**: whenever $x\sim_T y$, the join state $J_{ij}(x,y)$ is thermally equivalent to each of $x$ and $y$ under the nested-join identifications. The coordinate sum in the definition alone does not assert C1. In later theorem statements, T1–T5 and C1 are explicitly listed as hypotheses; they are not treated as established physical laws.

Let a simple domain and its finite thermal joins satisfy [[def-tdmath-forward-sector-hypotheses]] and [[def-tdmath-thermal-contact-hypotheses]]. Let $x_0\prec\prec x_1$ with $x_0\sim_T x_1$, and let $x$ satisfy $x_0\prec\prec x\prec\prec x_1$. For $0\le\lambda\le1$, write $R_\lambda$ for the compound state $((1-\lambda)x_0,\lambda x_1)$, omitting a zero coefficient at the endpoints. Then there is a unique $\lambda\in(0,1)$ with $R_\lambda\sim x$ in the common accessibility relation.

Under [[def-tdmath-forward-sector-hypotheses]], the sectors are nested: if $y\in A_x$, then $A_y\subseteq A_x$; equality holds when $y\in\partial A_x$, and $A_y\subset\operatorname{int}_{\Gamma_i}A_x$ when $y\in\operatorname{int}_{\Gamma_i}A_x$. For every $x,y\in\Gamma_i$, either $x\prec y$ or $y\prec x$ (possibly both). Strict comparison is exactly interior membership: $x\prec\prec y$ if and only if $y\in\operatorname{int}_{\Gamma_i}A_x$.

Let $u,v$ be finite-support real coefficient maps on the tagged state labels of [[def-tdmath-tagged-scalable-compound]] with equal total coefficient. For a typed state $x$, compound notation uses the represented map $\mathsf{J}(x)$ from [[def-tdmath-forward-sector-hypotheses]]; its raw unit point mass is $e_{(\Gamma,x)}$. Signed maps still use the ordinary total of their raw coefficients, exactly the bookkeeping mass of the represented nonnegative maps. Put $d=v-u$, $d^+(x)=\max(d(x),0)$ and $d^-(x)=\max(-d(x),0)$. Define $u\preceq_s v$ to mean $d^-\prec d^+$ under the compound relation of [[def-tdmath-forward-sector-hypotheses]]. Write $u\sim_s v$ when both $u\preceq_s v$ and $v\preceq_s u$. These are formal signed comparison maps, not physical negative amounts. The positive and negative parts are finite-support compounds of equal mass. If $u\sim_s v$, then $cu\sim_s cv$ for every real $c$: positive $c$ uses scaling, $c=0$ is reflexivity, and negative $c$ swaps the positive and negative parts while equivalence supplies both comparison directions. This Definition introduces the signed notation; ordinary-order compatibility and the signed-order laws are proved separately.

Under A1–A6 of [[def-tdmath-forward-sector-hypotheses]], for compounds $A,B$ with $m(A)=m(B)$ and every finite spectator compound $C$, $A+C\prec B+C$ if and only if $A\prec B$. Consequently, for finite-support signed maps $u,v$ of equal total coefficient, define $u\preceq_s v$ by $(v-u)^-\prec(v-u)^+$. This relation is well-defined, agrees with $\prec$ on nonnegative maps, is invariant under adding a common signed map, is transitive, and is closed under addition of two comparisons. No comparison hypothesis is used.

Under [[def-tdmath-forward-sector-hypotheses]], each simple domain has one orientation sign $\varepsilon_i\in\{-1,1\}$, constant across the domain, such that at fixed work coordinate $v$, $x\prec y$ exactly when $\varepsilon_i(u_y-u_x)\ge0$. In coordinates oriented so $\varepsilon_i=1$, for each $x\in\Gamma_i$ the projection $\rho_x$ of $\partial_{\Gamma_i}A_x$ onto work coordinates is open and connected; the boundary is the graph $(u_x(v),v)$ of a $C^1$ function with locally Lipschitz derivative

$$Du_x(v)=-P_i(u_x(v),v).$$

If $y\in\partial A_x$, then $A_y=A_x$ and their boundary graphs agree.

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$ with $n \ge 1$, let $\mathbb{R}^n$ be the set of functions
$n \to \mathbb{R}$ and let $d_2$ be the Euclidean metric on it
([[lem-metrics-on-rn]]). Then:

1. **Closed boxes are compact.** For reals $a_k \le b_k$ $(k < n)$ the box
   $Q = \{\, x \in \mathbb{R}^n : a_k \le x_k \le b_k \text{ for every } k < n \,\}$
   is a compact subset of $(\mathbb{R}^n, d_2)$ ([[def-metric-compactness]]).
2. **Heine-Borel.** A subset $K \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ is a compact subset of
   $(\mathbb{R}^n, d_2)$ if and only if $K$ is closed in $\mathbb{R}^n$
   ([[def-metric-topology]]) and bounded
   ([[def-metric-bounded-diameter]]).
3. **The real line.** A subset $K \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ is a compact subset of
   $(\mathbb{R}, d_{\mathbb{R}})$, the usual metric $d_{\mathbb{R}}(x,y) = |x-y|$
   ([[lem-real-line-is-a-metric-space]]), if and only if $K$ is closed in
   $\mathbb{R}$ and bounded.

**No choice principle is used.** The bisection below halves one coordinate at a
time and takes the **left** half whenever the left half still fails to be finitely
covered, the right half otherwise: a rule with two outcomes, decided by a
property of the box, not a selection. That is the whole reason the theorem is
available in ZF, while the general "complete and totally bounded implies compact"
([[thm-complete-and-totally-bounded-implies-compact]]) is not.

The hypothesis $n \ge 1$ is inherited from [[lem-metrics-on-rn]], which defines
$\mathbb{R}^n$ and its metrics only there; the last remark below records what
happens at $n = 0$.

derivations.claim: By T4, the open strips $\Sigma(a,b):=\{x:a\prec\prec x\prec\prec b\}$ with $a\prec\prec b$ and $a\sim_T b$ cover $\Gamma_i$. They are open: by [F2], $a\prec\prec x$ is $x\in\operatorname{int}A_a$, and $x\prec\prec b$ is $x\notin A_b$; the latter set is open because $A_b$ is relatively closed.

Let $\Sigma(a,b)$ and $\Sigma(c,d)$ overlap. Their intersection is open. Choose two states $e\prec\prec f$ in a small vertical segment contained in the overlap, using [F4]. Let $s_e,s_f$ be their coordinates in the first strip and $t_e,t_f$ in the second, supplied by [F1]. If $s_f<s_e$, the signed difference $R_{s_e}-R_{s_f}=(s_e-s_f)(\mathsf{J}(b)-\mathsf{J}(a))$ and positive scaling and signed compatibility [A1, F3] give $R_{s_f}\prec R_{s_e}$, so $f\prec e$ by the two reference equivalences; if $s_f=s_e$, those references coincide and give $f\sim e$. Both contradict $e\prec\prec f$. Hence $s_f>s_e$, and the same argument gives $t_f>t_e$.

The four reference equivalences give, in signed comparison,
$f-e\sim_s(s_f-s_e)(b-a),\qquad f-e\sim_s(t_f-t_e)(d-c).$
Put $r=(s_f-s_e)/(t_f-t_e)>0$. Additivity and positive scaling in [F3] give $d-c\sim_s r(b-a)$. Applying the same algebra to the equivalences for $e$ gives $c\sim_s a+(s_e-r t_e)(b-a)$. Consequently a state in the second strip with coordinate $t$ has first-chart coordinate $s_e+r(t-t_e)$. The change of chart is affine with strictly positive slope.

The same calculation covers a finite chain of overlapping strips: after each overlap, express the new strip's endpoint states as signed-equivalent affine maps in the existing reference pair. The local strip lemma gives every state $z$ of the added strip a coordinate $s_z\in\mathbb R$ with $\mathsf{J}(z)\sim_s(1-s_z)\mathsf{J}(a)+s_z\mathsf{J}(b)$ in the existing chart. Signed addition, positive scaling, translation, and equivalence under negative scaling are valid by [F3]; hence induction along a finite overlap chain gives one such common chart for every state in the union.

Take any finite list of target states in $\Gamma_i$ and join them in order by finitely many straight segments, which lie in $\Gamma_i$ by convexity. The resulting connected path is a finite union of closed bounded segments, hence compact by [F5]. The open strips from step 1.1 cover it, so compactness gives a finite subcover. The intersection graph of those strips meeting the path is connected: otherwise their unions would partition the connected path into two disjoint nonempty relatively open sets. Order a spanning tree from one root strip; each later strip overlaps an earlier one in an open set and can be glued by step 3.1. Thus every target state has a common signed chart $\mathsf{J}(z)\sim_s(1-s_z)\mathsf{J}(a)+s_z\mathsf{J}(b)$ with $a\prec\prec b$.

Write the arbitrary scaled-copy compounds as
$$A=\sum_j\alpha_j\mathsf{J}_{r_j\Gamma_i}(r_jx_j),\qquad B=\sum_k\beta_k\mathsf{J}_{h_k\Gamma_i}(h_ky_k),$$
with $r_j,h_k>0$ and nonnegative coefficients, omitting zero terms. The declared reversible transport in [A1] gives $\mathsf{J}_{r_j\Gamma_i}(r_jx_j)\sim r_j\mathsf{J}_{\Gamma_i}(x_j)$ and similarly on the other side; ordinary positive scaling and composition therefore reduce them to the unscaled base-type states with effective amounts $a_j=\alpha_jr_j$ and $b_k=\beta_kh_k$. Their masses are respectively $r_jw_{\Gamma_i}$ and $h_kw_{\Gamma_i}$ before this transport, so equal total mass $M$ implies
$$L=M/w_{\Gamma_i}=\sum_j a_j=\sum_k b_k.$$
If $M=0$, both maps are empty and reflexivity applies. Otherwise use step 4.1 for the finite list of base states $x_j,y_k$, with common-chart coordinates $s_j,t_k$. Signed addition and splitting [F3] make the transported compounds equivalent to $R_{q_A}=(L-q_A)\mathsf{J}(a)+q_A\mathsf{J}(b)$ and $R_{q_B}=(L-q_B)\mathsf{J}(a)+q_B\mathsf{J}(b)$, where $q_A=\sum_j a_js_j$ and $q_B=\sum_k b_kt_k$. If $q_A<q_B$, their signed difference has positive part $(q_B-q_A)\mathsf{J}(b)$ and negative part $(q_B-q_A)\mathsf{J}(a)$, so $a\prec b$ and positive scaling compare them; equality gives reflexivity, and $q_B<q_A$ gives the reverse comparison. Transitivity transfers this order through the reversible transports to the original distinct scaled tags. Hence CH holds for every allowed scaled-copy pair, without identifying those tags or dropping their scale factors.

For each simple type $\Gamma$ in that family, let $n_\Gamma\ge1$ and let $\Gamma\subset\mathbb R^{n_\Gamma+1}$ be nonempty, open and convex, with coordinates $x=(u,v)$. The notation for a type and its chart is shared, but each state has a distinct raw tag $(\Gamma,x)$. Scaled charts are distinct tagged copies $s\Gamma=\{sx:x\in\Gamma\}$ with coordinate transport $x\mapsto sx$; transported raw tags remain distinct from the original raw tags. Let $e_{(\Gamma,x)}$ be the unit point mass from [[def-tdmath-tagged-scalable-compound]]. The represented state is

$$\mathsf{J}_\Gamma(x):=w_\Gamma e_{(\Gamma,x)},\qquad m(\mathsf{J}_\Gamma(x))=w_\Gamma.$$

Write $\mathsf{J}(x):=\mathsf{J}_\Gamma(x)$ when $x$ already carries its type tag. All state notation in this framework's compound comparisons, including a bare $x$, denotes $\mathsf{J}_\Gamma(x)$; a raw unit point mass is always written $e_{(\Gamma,x)}$. A separated pair is addition of represented states, not a unit product tag. Nonnegative multiples are pointwise and zero terms are omitted. For an encoded compound $c$, its aggregate composition is the finite amount function

$$\nu(c):=\sum_{(\Gamma,x)\in\operatorname{supp}(c)}\frac{c(\Gamma,x)}{w_\Gamma}\nu_\Gamma;\qquad m(c)=\sum_{p\in P}\nu(c)(p).$$

Fix the formal interpretation $\Pi(c)$ as the finite separated preparation whose factor at each nonzero raw tag $(\Gamma,x)$ is the amount $c(\Gamma,x)/w_\Gamma$ of that typed state, using the declared coordinate scaling transport. The accessibility relation on coefficient maps is the pullback of the declared relation on these preparations. Merging or splitting repeated copies of the same preparation is reversible; permutation and reassociation preserve the preparation. Thus $\Pi(\mathsf{J}_{s\Gamma}(sx))$ and $\Pi(s\mathsf{J}_\Gamma(x))$ are the same declared scaled preparation and yield

$$\mathsf{J}_{s\Gamma}(sx)\sim s\mathsf{J}_\Gamma(x),$$

although their raw point masses have different tags and are not equal. This reversible transport commutes with finite composition, nested type constructors, and scaled splitting. It is part of the precise formal scaling interpretation, not a deduction about physical accessibility from coordinate multiplication. A physical use must adopt the stated preparation maps and accessibility assumptions; fixed-composition models compare only preparations with the same $\nu$, while a declared channel model may additionally compare different compositions of equal $m$.

A comparison $A\prec B$ is defined only when $m(A)=m(B)$, as in the coefficient-map supplier. Write $A\sim B$ when both directions hold, and $A\prec\prec B$ when only the forward direction holds. On any fixed simple type, dividing every represented state by the same positive constant $w_\Gamma$ gives its unit-point-mass comparison. Positive scaling and its inverse preserve and reflect order; whenever the required CH and reference hypotheses hold, the unit-state entropy theorem applies after that normalization. If $S$ represents unit-point-mass comparisons, the entropy of a represented state is $w_\Gamma S(x)$ and the entropy of a finite sum $\sum_j t_j\mathsf{J}_\Gamma(x_j)$ is $\sum_j t_j w_\Gamma S(x_j)$. No independent rescaling across different types is assumed without a calibrator.

The common relation satisfies A1–A6 on all equal-mass finite compounds: (A1) reflexivity; (A2) transitivity; (A3) if $A\prec B$, then $A+C\prec B+C$ for every compound $C$; (A4) if $A\prec B$, then $tA\prec tB$ for every $t>0$; (A5) $t\mathsf{J}_\Gamma(x)$ is equivalent to $s\mathsf{J}_\Gamma(x)+(t-s)\mathsf{J}_\Gamma(x)$ for $t>0$ and $0<s<t$, with the reversible scaled-copy transport above; (A6) for equal-mass $A,B$, fixed positive equal-mass spectators $Z_0,Z_1$, and every sequence $\epsilon_n>0$ decreasing to zero, $A+\epsilon_n Z_0\prec B+\epsilon_n Z_1$ for all $n$ implies $A\prec B$. These are hypotheses, not conclusions. No comparison hypothesis is included here.

For each $i$ and $x\in\Gamma_i$, define the forward sector $A_x:=\{y\in\Gamma_i:\mathsf{J}_{\Gamma_i}(x)\prec\mathsf{J}_{\Gamma_i}(y)\}$. The simple-domain assumptions are: (A7) for $x,y\in\Gamma_i$ and $0<t<1$, the encoded compound $t\mathsf{J}_{\Gamma_i}(x)+(1-t)\mathsf{J}_{\Gamma_i}(y)$ compares to $\mathsf{J}_{\Gamma_i}(tx+(1-t)y)$; both have bookkeeping mass $w_{\Gamma_i}$, and convexity puts the recombined coordinate in the chart; (S1) each $x$ has a strict successor; (S2) $A_x$ has exactly one supporting hyperplane at $x$, expressible as $u-u_x+P_i(x)\cdot(v-v_x)=0$ with a finite-valued slope map $P_i:\Gamma_i\to\mathbb R^{n_i}$, and $P_i$ is locally Lipschitz; (S3) the boundary of $A_x$ relative to $\Gamma_i$ is arcwise connected. A supporting hyperplane means that $A_x$ lies in one of its closed half-spaces and meets the plane at $x$. The affine hull is the smallest affine subspace containing a set; relative interior is interior in that affine hull. Closure and boundary are taken in the indicated affine hull or in $\Gamma_i$, as named; boundary is closure intersected with closure of the complement in that relative topology.

This definition imposes no physical interpretation, units, or empirical claim. A contact theorem that uses joins must separately assume that each join is a simple domain satisfying these same forward-sector hypotheses.

Under [[def-tdmath-forward-sector-hypotheses]], for every simple state $x$, the forward sector $A_x=\{y\in\Gamma_i:x\prec y\}$ is convex and closed relative to $\Gamma_i$. For collinear $y=tx+(1-t)z$, $0<t<1$, $y\prec z$ implies $x\prec y$, and $x\prec z$ implies $x\prec y$.
Under [[def-tdmath-forward-sector-hypotheses]], every forward sector $A_x$ has nonempty interior in its ambient simple domain $\Gamma_i$.

Under [[def-tdmath-forward-sector-hypotheses]], each simple domain has one orientation sign $\varepsilon_i\in\{-1,1\}$, constant across the domain, such that at fixed work coordinate $v$, $x\prec y$ exactly when $\varepsilon_i(u_y-u_x)\ge0$. In coordinates oriented so $\varepsilon_i=1$, for each $x\in\Gamma_i$ the projection $\rho_x$ of $\partial_{\Gamma_i}A_x$ onto work coordinates is open and connected; the boundary is the graph $(u_x(v),v)$ of a $C^1$ function with locally Lipschitz derivative

$$Du_x(v)=-P_i(u_x(v),v).$$

If $y\in\partial A_x$, then $A_y=A_x$ and their boundary graphs agree.

Let $C$ be a nonempty convex subset of a finite-dimensional affine Euclidean space $H$. Its relative interior $\operatorname{ri}_H C$ is the interior in $H=\operatorname{aff}C$. Then $\operatorname{ri}_H C$ is nonempty. If $w\in\operatorname{ri}_H C$, $y\in\overline{C}^{\,H}$, and $0\le t<1$, then $(1-t)w+ty\in\operatorname{ri}_H C$.

derivations.claim: If $y\in A_x$, transitivity gives $A_y\subseteq A_x$. If also $y\in\partial A_x$, [F3] gives equality. Suppose instead $y\in\operatorname{int}A_x$. If $A_y$ met $\partial A_x$ at $z$, then $z\in A_y$ and [F3] would give $A_z=A_x$. Since $z\in A_y$, transitivity gives $A_z\subseteq A_y\subseteq A_x$, so $A_y=A_x$. But S2 puts $y$ on $\partial A_y$, contradicting $y\in\operatorname{int}A_x$. Thus $A_y$ avoids $\partial A_x$ and, being a subset of the closed sector $A_x$, lies in $\operatorname{int}A_x$.

Suppose neither $y\in A_x$ nor $x\in A_y$. Choose $z\in\operatorname{int}A_x$ using [F2]. The segment from $y$ to $z$ lies in $\Gamma_i$ and meets $\partial A_x$ at a point $w$ strictly between its endpoints. By [F3], $A_w=A_x$, so $w\prec z$. The collinear implication in [F1], applied to $w=ty+(1-t)z$, gives $y\prec w\prec z$. Hence every $z\in\operatorname{int}A_x$ lies in $A_y$. Reversing $x,y$ gives $\operatorname{int}A_y\subseteq A_x$.

Because $A_x$ is full-dimensional by [F2], its affine hull is the ambient space. Fix $w\in\operatorname{int}A_x$. For any $q\in A_x$, relative closedness gives $q\in\overline{A_x}^{\,\Gamma_i}$, and [F4] puts $(1-t)w+tq$ in $\operatorname{int}A_x$ for every $0\le t<1$. Letting $t\uparrow1$ shows $q\in\overline{\operatorname{int}A_x}^{\,\Gamma_i}$. The reverse inclusion follows because $A_x$ is relatively closed. Hence $A_x=\overline{\operatorname{int}A_x}^{\,\Gamma_i}$; the same holds for $A_y$. Relative closedness from [F1] therefore extends the two interior inclusions in step 1.2 to $A_x\subseteq A_y$ and $A_y\subseteq A_x$. Equality would put $x\in A_y$, contradicting the supposition. Thus at least one of $x\prec y$ or $y\prec x$ always holds.

If $x\prec y$, then $y\in A_x$. If $y$ is a boundary point, step 1.1 gives $A_x=A_y$, hence $x\prec y$ and $y\prec x$. Otherwise step 1.1 gives $A_y\subset\operatorname{int}A_x$, and $x\notin A_y$ because S2 places $x$ on $\partial A_x$. Thus $x\prec\prec y$. Conversely, if $y\in\operatorname{int}A_x$, step 1.1 and S2 show $x\notin A_y$, so $x\prec\prec y$.

derivations.claim: Let $S_N=\{0,\ldots,N-1\}^d$ be the cell indices in $\Lambda_N$. For $i\in S_N$, set $A_{i,N}=\{j-i:j\in S_N,\ j<_{\rm lex}i\}$; this is a finite subset of the past of the reference cell. Repeated conditional-density factorization from [F3] gives, $P$-almost surely, $$\log h_N(\omega)=\sum_{i\in S_N}\log k_{A_{i,N}}(T_{-i}\omega).$$ Every finite factor is defined $P$-almost surely because the corresponding local relative entropy is finite by [F1].

Fix $\varepsilon>0$. By the directed convergence in [F2], choose a finite past $A_*$ such that every finite $B\supseteq A_*$ satisfies $E_P|\log k_B-Z|<\varepsilon$. Put $R=\max\{|a_j|:a\in A_*,1\leq j\leq d\}$, with $R=0$ if $A_*=\varnothing$. Let $S_N^\circ$ consist of cells at least $R$ cells from each face of $S_N$. If $i\in S_N^\circ$, then $A_*\subseteq A_{i,N}$, so by stationarity $E_P|\log k_{A_{i,N}}(T_{-i}\omega)-Z(T_{-i}\omega)|<\varepsilon$. The boundary has $N^d-(N-2R)^d=o(N^d)$ cells (for $N>2R$). For every finite past $B$, $E_P\log k_B=g(B)\leq\gamma$ and $E_P(-\log k_B)^+\leq1/e$, hence $E_P|\log k_B|\leq\gamma+2/e$. For $Z=\log k_\infty$, $E_P(-\log k_\infty)^+=\int_{0<k_\infty<1}k_\infty(-\log k_\infty)\,dR_0\leq1/e$ on its reference probability $R_0=P_{F_+}\otimes Q_C$, so [F2] gives $E_P|Z|\leq\gamma+2/e$ as well. Summing the interior errors and bounding each boundary error by $2(\gamma+2/e)$ yields $$\left\|N^{-d}\log h_N-N^{-d}\sum_{i\in S_N}Z(T_{-i}\cdot)\right\|_{L^1(P)}\longrightarrow0,$$ since $\varepsilon$ was arbitrary.

For $j=1,\ldots,d$, the shift $U_jf=f\circ T_{-e_j}$ is a linear isometry on complex $L^2(P)$ by stationarity. Apply [F4] to $N^{-1}\sum_{n=0}^{N-1}U_j^n$, obtaining strong convergence to the orthogonal projection $P_j$ onto the $U_j$-invariant subspace. The coordinate shifts commute, so every average for coordinate $j$ commutes with every average for coordinate $k$; taking strong limits shows that the $P_j$ commute with each other and with the other coordinate averages. Since all these operators have norm at most one, a finite telescoping estimate gives strong convergence of the product of the $d$ averages to $P_1\cdots P_d$. This product is the orthogonal projection onto the intersection of the coordinate-invariant subspaces, because the $P_j$ are commuting orthogonal projections. The product averages are exactly the rectangular cube averages $N^{-d}\sum_{i\in S_N}Z_M(T_{-i}\cdot)$, so these converge in $L^2$ for bounded $Z_M$ to a function invariant under every integer shift.

Since $Z\in L^1(P)$, dominated convergence gives $\|Z-Z_M\|_1\to0$. Cube averages are $L^1$ contractions, so the averages of $Z$ are Cauchy in $L^1$: for large $M$ their distance from the convergent averages of $Z_M$ is at most $\|Z-Z_M\|_1$. Let their $L^1$ limit be $s$. Every cube average has mean $E_PZ=\gamma$, hence $E_Ps=\gamma$. For each coordinate shift $e_j$, the averaging index cube and its translate have symmetric difference of exactly $2N^{d-1}$ indices, so $\|U_j A_NZ-A_NZ\|_1\leq2\|Z\|_1/N$. Passing to the $L^1$ limit gives $U_js=s$. These generators imply invariance under every integer translation.

Fix $r\in\mathbb R^d$, put $G=\Lambda_N$, $G'=G+r$, and $B=G\cap G'$. For $N>2\|r\|_\infty$, $B$ contains a cube $J$ of side $N-2\|r\|_\infty$. By [F1] and restriction monotonicity, $D(P_G\Vert Q_G)\leq\gamma N^d$ and $D(P_B\Vert Q_B)\geq D(P_J\Vert Q_J)$; the latter divided by $N^d$ tends to $\gamma$. Therefore $N^{-d}(D(P_G\Vert Q_G)-D(P_B\Vert Q_B))\to0$. The conditional chain rule [F3] identifies $\log h_G-\log h_B$ with a conditional log density. Its mean is this entropy difference, and [F3] bounds its negative-part expectation by $1/e$; thus its $L^1(P)$ norm is at most the entropy difference plus $2/e$. The same bound applies to $G'$. Translation covariance gives $\log h_{G'}=(\log h_G)\circ T_{-r}$; thus the normalized information in $G$ and $G'$ have the same $L^1$ limit. Since $N^{-d}\log h_G\to s$, it follows that $s\circ T_{-r}=s$ $P$-almost surely for this $r$.

Step 5.1 applies to every fixed $r\in\mathbb R^d$. For each rational $q$, the event $\{s\leq q\}$ is therefore invariant modulo null sets under every translation. Full-translation ergodicity makes each such event have probability $0$ or $1$. If $s$ were not almost surely constant, some rational sublevel set would have probability strictly between $0$ and $1$; hence $s$ is constant. Its mean from step 4.1 is $\gamma$, so $s=\gamma$. Combining with step 2.1 proves the asserted $L^1(P)$ limit.

Assume AC. Let $d\geq1$, let $P\in\mathcal P^1_{\rm stat}(\Omega)$, with this class defined in [[def-tdmath-local-tame-topology]], be ergodic under the full translation group $\mathbb R^d$, and suppose its specific relative entropy $I(P)=\gamma$ relative to the unit-intensity Poisson law $Q$ is finite. Ergodic means that every measurable event invariant modulo $P$-null sets under each translation has probability $0$ or $1$. Assume the Axiom of Choice and fix an integer dimension $d\geq1$. For $i\in\mathbb Z^d$, let $C_i=i+[0,1)^d$. These are left-closed, right-open cells. For every $x\in\mathbb R^d$, [[lem-integer-part]] supplies the unique integers $i_j$ with $i_j\le x_j<i_j+1$, so $x$ belongs to exactly one $C_i$. The cells are Borel products of closed/open ray intersections and have volume one by [[thm-lebesgue-measure-of-a-box-of-every-kind]], whose statement covers this face convention. A finite configuration in $C_i$ is a finite subset of distinct points. Encode it by its cardinality $n\in\mathbb N_0$ and its uniquely lexicographically increasing list of local coordinates $(x_1-i,\ldots,x_n-i)\in([0,1)^d)^n$. Pad the code after its first $n$ coordinates with the zero vector. For fixed $n$, the strictly increasing lists form a Borel subset of $([0,1]^d)^n$, since lexicographic strict order is a finite union of coordinate-equality and coordinate-inequality conditions. Thus all codes form a Borel subset of $\mathbb N_0\times([0,1]^d)^{\mathbb N}$. Each factor $[0,1]^d$ is Polish as a closed subspace of complete $\mathbb R^d$ with a countable dense rational grid; $\mathbb N_0$ with its discrete metric is Polish. The ambient space is Polish by [[cor-countable-products-and-g-delta-subspaces-of-polish-spaces-are-polish]] (and is completely metrized by [[lem-standard-complete-metric-on-a-countable-product]]), so [[lem-borel-subspaces-admit-polish-presentations]] makes the cell space $E_i$ standard Borel. By [[lem-tdmath-counts-generate-configuration-sigma]], its sigma-algebra is generated by the counts $N_B$ for Borel $B\subseteq C_i$.

For $\lambda>0$, give a cell configuration with $n$ points probability $e^{-\lambda}\lambda^n/n!$ for its count. The probabilities sum to one by the exponential power series and addition formula. Conditional on count $n$, take the $n$-fold product of normalized Lebesgue measure on $C_i$, restrict it to the complement of the collision diagonals, and push it forward by lexicographic sorting. The product exists by the finite product-measure theorem; each collision diagonal is null by Tonelli and the fact that Lebesgue measure gives every singleton measure zero, so the restricted measure still has mass one. Sorting is Borel on the finitely many permutation regions of the no-collision set. This defines a law $\pi_{i,\lambda}$ on $E_i$; for $n=0$, use the empty product and the empty configuration. Let $\Omega=\prod_{i\in\mathbb Z^d}E_i$ with its product cylinder sigma-algebra. The product sigma-algebra is generated by the cell-coordinate sigma-algebras, each generated by counts on Borel subsets of its bounded cell by [[lem-tdmath-counts-generate-configuration-sigma]]. Conversely every bounded-region count is a finite sum of these cell counts, since a bounded set meets finitely many cells. Thus the product cylinder sigma-algebra is exactly the sigma-algebra generated by all bounded-Borel count maps. For each $\lambda>0$, $Q_\lambda$ denotes the unique probability on $\Omega$ whose finite cell marginals are the products of the corresponding $\pi_{i,\lambda}$. Existence and uniqueness follow from [[thm-kolmogorov-extension-for-standard-borel-coordinate-spaces]]. In particular every translation $T_x$ is measurable since $N_A(T_x\omega)=N_{A-x}(\omega)$. The unit-intensity reference is $Q:=Q_1$.

Identify each $\omega\in\Omega$ with the simple locally finite counting measure obtained by uniting its finite cell configurations. For a bounded Borel set $A\subseteq\mathbb R^d$, write $N_A(\omega)=\omega(A)$ and $|A|$ for its Lebesgue measure. Define translation by $T_x\omega(A)=\omega(A-x)$ for $x\in\mathbb R^d$. The next item proves that under $Q_\lambda$, counts in disjoint bounded Borel sets are independent Poisson random variables with means $\lambda|A|$ and that $Q_\lambda$ is translation invariant. This item is a mathematical reference construction and makes no physical claim.

Define the intensity measure on Borel sets by $\Lambda_{Q_\lambda}(A):=E_{Q_\lambda}N_A$, where $N_A=\omega(A)$ and the nonnegative expectation may be infinite. For pairwise disjoint bounded Borel sets $A_1,\ldots,A_r\subseteq\mathbb R^d$, the restrictions $\omega|_{A_1},\ldots,\omega|_{A_r}$ are independent, each count $N_{A_j}$ has Poisson law with mean $\lambda|A_j|$, and the joint law of counts on any finite disjoint family is the product of those Poisson laws. In particular, $Q_\lambda$ is invariant under every translation $T_x$, and $\Lambda_{Q_\lambda}(A)=\lambda|A|$ for every Borel $A$. For every bounded Borel $A$ and real $a$, its count also has the exact exponential moment
$$E_{Q_\lambda}e^{aN_A}=\exp\!\left(\lambda|A|(e^a-1)\right).$$

derivations.claim: If $G_1,G_2$ are disjoint bounded Borel sets, [F1] decomposes $D(P_{G_1\cup G_2}\Vert Q_{G_1}\otimes Q_{G_2})$ into $D(P_{G_1}\Vert Q_{G_1})$ plus the mean conditional relative entropy of $G_2$ given $G_1$. That conditional increment is at least $D(P_{G_2}\Vert Q_{G_2})$ by the conditioning monotonicity in [F1], comparing observation by $G_1$ with no observation. Thus relative entropy is superadditive over disjoint regions; if the left side is infinite the inequality is immediate, and otherwise all terms in the chain rule are finite.

Fix an integer $m\geq1$ and let $q_N=\lfloor N/m\rfloor$. Tile $[0,q_Nm)^d$ by $q_N^d$ disjoint translates of $\Lambda_m$, leaving the Borel remainder $\Lambda_N\setminus[0,q_Nm)^d$. Iterating step 1.1 and using nonnegativity on the remainder gives $$D(P_{\Lambda_N}\Vert Q_{\Lambda_N})\geq q_N^dD(P_{\Lambda_m}\Vert Q_{\Lambda_m}),$$ because stationarity gives the same entropy for each translated $m$-cube. If $D(P_{\Lambda_m}\Vert Q_{\Lambda_m})=+\infty$, this forces $D(P_{\Lambda_N}\Vert Q_{\Lambda_N})=+\infty$ for every $N\geq m$.

Put $s=\sup_{m\geq1}m^{-d}D(P_{\Lambda_m}\Vert Q_{\Lambda_m})$. If $s=+\infty$, step 2.1 makes the liminf of $N^{-d}D_N$ exceed every finite bound, so the integer-cube limit is $+\infty=s$. If $s<+\infty$, step 2.1 gives $$\liminf_{N\to\infty}N^{-d}D_N\geq m^{-d}D(P_{\Lambda_m}\Vert Q_{\Lambda_m})$$ for every $m$, since $q_N^d/N^d\to m^{-d}$. Taking the supremum gives liminf at least $s$, while the definition of $s$ gives $N^{-d}D_N\leq s$ for every integer $N$. Hence the integer-cube limit exists and equals $s$.

For real $L\to\infty$, let $N=\lfloor L\rfloor$. The inclusions $\Lambda_N\subseteq\Lambda_L\subseteq\Lambda_{N+1}$ and [F3] give $D_N\leq D_L\leq D_{N+1}$. Since $N/L\to1$ and $(N+1)/L\to1$, step 3.1 squeezes $L^{-d}D_L$ to the same extended limit $s$; if some integer-cube entropy is infinite, monotonicity gives the same conclusion directly.

If $I(P)<\infty$ and $A$ is bounded, choose an integer cube $\Lambda_N+x$ containing $A$. Stationarity [F2] and restriction monotonicity [F3] give $$D(P_A\Vert Q_A)\leq D(P_{\Lambda_N+x}\Vert Q_{\Lambda_N+x})=D(P_{\Lambda_N}\Vert Q_{\Lambda_N})\leq N^d I(P)<\infty.$$ Thus every bounded restriction has finite relative entropy.

Assume AC and let $P\in\mathcal P^1_{\rm stat}(\Omega)$, with this class defined in [[def-tdmath-local-tame-topology]], be stationary for the translations of [[def-tdmath-poisson-configuration-reference]]. For a bounded Borel set $G$, write $P_G$ and $Q_G$ for the restrictions of $P$ and the unit-intensity Poisson reference $Q$ to configurations in $G$. For $L>0$, put $\Lambda_L=[0,L)^d$ and
$$D_L:=D(P_{\Lambda_L}\Vert Q_{\Lambda_L}).$$
Then the specific relative entropy density
$$I(P):=\lim_{L\to\infty}\frac{D_L}{L^d}$$
exists in $[0,+\infty]$ and satisfies
$$I(P)=\sup_{m\in\mathbb N,\ m\geq1}\frac{D(P_{\Lambda_m}\Vert Q_{\Lambda_m})}{m^d}.$$
If $I(P)<\infty$, every bounded Borel restriction has finite relative entropy. This is an information functional relative to the specified unit-intensity Poisson law; changing the reference changes its value.

Set $\alpha:=\frac12\bigl(1+d/(d+\epsilon)\bigr)$ and
$g_\ell:=\ell^\alpha$. Then $d/(d+\epsilon)<\alpha<1$ and
$\ell^d g_\ell^{-d-\epsilon}=\ell^{d-\alpha(d+\epsilon)}\to0$ while
$g_\ell/\ell\to0$. Fix a sufficiently large $\ell\ge1$ so that
$g_\ell\ge R$. For $L\ge\ell+g_\ell$, set
$m_L:=\lfloor L/(\ell+g_\ell)\rfloor$. Since $L/(\ell+g_\ell)\ge1$, [F10]
gives $m_L\ge1$ and
$m_L(\ell+g_\ell)\le L<(m_L+1)(\ell+g_\ell)$. Place $M_L=m_L^d$ cubes
$$C_j=(\ell+g_\ell)j+[0,\ell]^d,\qquad j\in\{0,\ldots,m_L-1\}^d.$$
They lie inside $[0,L]^d$ and have pairwise gaps at least $g_\ell$.

Fix occupancies $0\le N_j\le n_\ell$ with total $N=\sum_jN_j$. The
ordered configurations in the disjoint cubes with exactly these occupancies
are partitioned by assignments of the $N$ particle labels to cubes. The number
of assignments is $N!/(\prod_jN_j!)$: order all $N$ labels, then note that
each assignment occurs exactly $\prod_jN_j!$ times from within-cube reorderings.
Particle-permutation symmetry of $U_N$ and invariance of the finite product
measure (rectangle formula and uniqueness in [F6]) make the assignment
integrals equal.

Restrict the grand partition sum in $[0,L]^d$ to configurations with no
particles outside these cubes and at most $n_\ell$ particles in each cube,
where $n_\ell$ is the cutoff from [F2]. If two cubes have index difference
$k\ne0$, the coordinate gap in a coordinate attaining $\|k\|_\infty$ is at
least $\|k\|_\infty g_\ell$; [F3] therefore bounds the total absolute
inter-cube energy by
$$D_L\le\frac C2M_Ln_\ell^2S_{d,\epsilon}g_\ell^{-d-\epsilon}.$$
Thus $U_N=\sum_jU_{N_j}^{(j)}+U_{\mathrm{cross}}$ with
$U_{\mathrm{cross}}\le D_L$, and
$e^{-\beta U_N}\ge e^{-\beta D_L}\prod_j e^{-\beta U_{N_j}^{(j)}}$;
this remains true when an internal energy is $+\infty$, since both sides then
vanish.

On each assignment domain from step 2.1, the pointwise lower bound in
step 2.2 factors into nonnegative within-cube integrands. Repeated application
of [F5] and the rectangle formula in [F6] factors their integral into the
product of the translated one-cube integrals; [F7] identifies each with its
origin-centered value. Multiplying by $a^N/N!$ cancels the label count from
step 2.1, leaving $e^{-\beta D_L}\prod_j Z_{\ell,N_j}$. Summing over the
finitely many occupancy vectors and expanding the finite product of cutoff
sums from [F2] gives
$$\Xi_L\ge e^{-\beta D_L}(\Xi_\ell^{\mathrm{cut}})^{M_L}.$$

The integer-part bounds in step 1.1 give
$L/(\ell+g_\ell)-1<m_L\le L/(\ell+g_\ell)$, so
$m_L/L\to(\ell+g_\ell)^{-1}$ and $M_L/L^d\to(\ell+g_\ell)^{-d}$.
By [F2], $\Xi_\ell^{\mathrm{cut}}\ge(1-e^{-\ell^d})\Xi_\ell$, so
$\log\Xi_\ell^{\mathrm{cut}}\ge\ell^dp_\ell+\log(1-e^{-\ell^d})$.
Taking logarithms in step 3.1, dividing by $L^d$, and using step 2.2 gives
$$p_L\ge\frac{M_L}{L^d}\left(\ell^dp_\ell+\log(1-e^{-\ell^d})-\frac{\beta C}{2}n_\ell^2S_{d,\epsilon}g_\ell^{-d-\epsilon}\right).$$
Taking the lower limit and using the volume ratio above yields the same bound
with $M_L/L^d$ replaced by $(\ell+g_\ell)^{-d}$. The cutoff definition [F2]
and $\ell\ge1$ give
$n_\ell\le K\ell^d+1\le(K+1)\ell^d$. Factoring
$(\ell/(\ell+g_\ell))^d$ and using this estimate in the negative error term
therefore gives
$$\liminf_{L\to\infty}p_L\ge\left(\frac{\ell}{\ell+g_\ell}\right)^d\left[p_\ell+\ell^{-d}\log(1-e^{-\ell^d})-\frac{\beta C}{2}(K+1)^2S_{d,\epsilon}\ell^dg_\ell^{-d-\epsilon}\right].$$

As $\ell\to\infty$, the prefactor tends to $1$. Also
$e^{-\ell^d}\to0$, so continuity of $\log$ at $1$ gives
$\log(1-e^{-\ell^d})\to0$; since $\ell^{-d}\to0$, their product
$\ell^{-d}\log(1-e^{-\ell^d})$ tends to zero. The cross-energy error tends to
zero because $d-\alpha(d+\epsilon)<0$ by step 1.1. The replacement of the
prefactor times $p_\ell$ by $p_\ell$ has error at most
$Q\bigl[1-(\ell/(\ell+g_\ell))^d\bigr]\to0$ by [F2]. Thus for every
$\eta>0$ there is $T$ such that every $\ell\ge T$ makes the right side of
step 4.1 at least $p_\ell-\eta$.

Let $\overline p=\limsup_{\ell\to\infty}p_\ell$. By [A1], for every
$\eta>0$ and every $T\ge1$ there is an $\ell\ge T$ with
$p_\ell>\overline p-\eta$; otherwise the tail supremum from $T$ onward would
be at most $\overline p-\eta$, contradicting the infimum defining
$\overline p$. Choose $T$ large enough for step 5.1. Then
$\liminf_{L\to\infty}p_L\ge\overline p-2\eta$. Letting $\eta\downarrow0$
shows $\liminf p_L\ge\limsup p_L$.

For any $S,T\ge1$, choose $L\ge\max(S,T)$. Then
$\inf_{x\ge S}p_x\le p_L\le\sup_{x\ge T}p_x$. Taking the supremum over $S$
and then the infimum over $T$ proves
$\liminf p_L\le\limsup p_L$ by [A1]. Together with step 6.1, the two finite
tail bounds equal a number $p$. For every $\eta>0$, their definitions give
tail thresholds with $\inf_{L\ge T_-}p_L>p-\eta$ and
$\sup_{L\ge T_+}p_L<p+\eta$; hence $|p_L-p|<\eta$ for all sufficiently large
$L$. The limit is finite by [F2]. This proves existence for the specified
free-cube reduced grand pressure.

$\Xi_L(a,\beta)$ defined in

$$p(a,\beta):=\lim_{L\to\infty}p_L(a,\beta)$$
exists as a finite real number. The assertion is for cubes with free boundary
and the displayed power-tail hypothesis.

Let $P$ be a set of primitive type labels. A formal type $\Gamma$ records a finitely supported amount function $\nu_\Gamma:P\to\mathbb R_{\ge0}$, not identically zero. Primitive generators have their unit amount function. Positive scaling, separated product, and thermal-join constructors retain distinct formal tags and obey

$$\nu_{s\Gamma}=s\nu_\Gamma,\qquad \nu_{\Gamma\otimes\Gamma'}=\nu_\Gamma+\nu_{\Gamma'}\qquad(s>0).$$

Separated and joined types are distinct constructors even when their amount functions agree. Permutation, reassociation, and scaled-splitting conventions preserve the amount function. Define the positive **bookkeeping weight** $w_\Gamma:=\sum_{p\in P}\nu_\Gamma(p)$, a finite sum over support. Thus $w_{s\Gamma}=s w_\Gamma$ and every product or join has weight $w_\Gamma+w_{\Gamma'}$. The optional empty unit has zero amount function and weight zero; it is represented only by the empty compound, not as a simple chart. These are formal amounts, not masses in kilograms or an empirical conservation law. The functions and pointwise operations use [[def-function-space]]; their finite-support convention and finite sums are those of [[def-tdmath-tagged-scalable-compound]] and [[lem-tdmath-compound-mass-well-defined]].

Let $I$ index the declared family of simple types $\Gamma_i$. For each simple type $\Gamma$ in that family, let $n_\Gamma\ge1$ and let $\Gamma\subset\mathbb R^{n_\Gamma+1}$ be nonempty, open and convex, with coordinates $x=(u,v)$. The notation for a type and its chart is shared, but each state has a distinct raw tag $(\Gamma,x)$. Scaled charts are distinct tagged copies $s\Gamma=\{sx:x\in\Gamma\}$ with coordinate transport $x\mapsto sx$; transported raw tags remain distinct from the original raw tags. Let $e_{(\Gamma,x)}$ be the unit point mass from [[def-tdmath-tagged-scalable-compound]]. The represented state is

$$\mathsf{J}_\Gamma(x):=w_\Gamma e_{(\Gamma,x)},\qquad m(\mathsf{J}_\Gamma(x))=w_\Gamma.$$

Write $\mathsf{J}(x):=\mathsf{J}_\Gamma(x)$ when $x$ already carries its type tag. All state notation in this framework's compound comparisons, including a bare $x$, denotes $\mathsf{J}_\Gamma(x)$; a raw unit point mass is always written $e_{(\Gamma,x)}$. A separated pair is addition of represented states, not a unit product tag. Nonnegative multiples are pointwise and zero terms are omitted. For an encoded compound $c$, its aggregate composition is the finite amount function

$$\nu(c):=\sum_{(\Gamma,x)\in\operatorname{supp}(c)}\frac{c(\Gamma,x)}{w_\Gamma}\nu_\Gamma;\qquad m(c)=\sum_{p\in P}\nu(c)(p).$$

Fix the formal interpretation $\Pi(c)$ as the finite separated preparation whose factor at each nonzero raw tag $(\Gamma,x)$ is the amount $c(\Gamma,x)/w_\Gamma$ of that typed state, using the declared coordinate scaling transport. The accessibility relation on coefficient maps is the pullback of the declared relation on these preparations. Merging or splitting repeated copies of the same preparation is reversible; permutation and reassociation preserve the preparation. Thus $\Pi(\mathsf{J}_{s\Gamma}(sx))$ and $\Pi(s\mathsf{J}_\Gamma(x))$ are the same declared scaled preparation and yield

$$\mathsf{J}_{s\Gamma}(sx)\sim s\mathsf{J}_\Gamma(x),$$

although their raw point masses have different tags and are not equal. This reversible transport commutes with finite composition, nested type constructors, and scaled splitting. It is part of the precise formal scaling interpretation, not a deduction about physical accessibility from coordinate multiplication. A physical use must adopt the stated preparation maps and accessibility assumptions; fixed-composition models compare only preparations with the same $\nu$, while a declared channel model may additionally compare different compositions of equal $m$.

A comparison $A\prec B$ is defined only when $m(A)=m(B)$, as in the coefficient-map supplier. Write $A\sim B$ when both directions hold, and $A\prec\prec B$ when only the forward direction holds. On any fixed simple type, dividing every represented state by the same positive constant $w_\Gamma$ gives its unit-point-mass comparison. Positive scaling and its inverse preserve and reflect order; whenever the required CH and reference hypotheses hold, the unit-state entropy theorem applies after that normalization. If $S$ represents unit-point-mass comparisons, the entropy of a represented state is $w_\Gamma S(x)$ and the entropy of a finite sum $\sum_j t_j\mathsf{J}_\Gamma(x_j)$ is $\sum_j t_j w_\Gamma S(x_j)$. No independent rescaling across different types is assumed without a calibrator.

The common relation satisfies A1–A6 on all equal-mass finite compounds: (A1) reflexivity; (A2) transitivity; (A3) if $A\prec B$, then $A+C\prec B+C$ for every compound $C$; (A4) if $A\prec B$, then $tA\prec tB$ for every $t>0$; (A5) $t\mathsf{J}_\Gamma(x)$ is equivalent to $s\mathsf{J}_\Gamma(x)+(t-s)\mathsf{J}_\Gamma(x)$ for $t>0$ and $0<s<t$, with the reversible scaled-copy transport above; (A6) for equal-mass $A,B$, fixed positive equal-mass spectators $Z_0,Z_1$, and every sequence $\epsilon_n>0$ decreasing to zero, $A+\epsilon_n Z_0\prec B+\epsilon_n Z_1$ for all $n$ implies $A\prec B$. These are hypotheses, not conclusions. No comparison hypothesis is included here.

For each $i$ and $x\in\Gamma_i$, define the forward sector $A_x:=\{y\in\Gamma_i:\mathsf{J}_{\Gamma_i}(x)\prec\mathsf{J}_{\Gamma_i}(y)\}$. The simple-domain assumptions are: (A7) for $x,y\in\Gamma_i$ and $0<t<1$, the encoded compound $t\mathsf{J}_{\Gamma_i}(x)+(1-t)\mathsf{J}_{\Gamma_i}(y)$ compares to $\mathsf{J}_{\Gamma_i}(tx+(1-t)y)$; both have bookkeeping mass $w_{\Gamma_i}$, and convexity puts the recombined coordinate in the chart; (S1) each $x$ has a strict successor; (S2) $A_x$ has exactly one supporting hyperplane at $x$, expressible as $u-u_x+P_i(x)\cdot(v-v_x)=0$ with a finite-valued slope map $P_i:\Gamma_i\to\mathbb R^{n_i}$, and $P_i$ is locally Lipschitz; (S3) the boundary of $A_x$ relative to $\Gamma_i$ is arcwise connected. A supporting hyperplane means that $A_x$ lies in one of its closed half-spaces and meets the plane at $x$. The affine hull is the smallest affine subspace containing a set; relative interior is interior in that affine hull. Closure and boundary are taken in the indicated affine hull or in $\Gamma_i$, as named; boundary is closure intersected with closure of the complement in that relative topology.

This definition imposes no physical interpretation, units, or empirical claim. A contact theorem that uses joins must separately assume that each join is a simple domain satisfying these same forward-sector hypotheses.

Let $I$ be a nonempty set of primitive simple-system labels containing a distinguished meter label $m$. Assume every finite separated product is explicitly represented by its finitely many tagged elementary factors; positive scaling and finite product are the only identifications. Suppose the join-closed family satisfies the hypotheses of [[thm-tdmath-conditional-contact-calibrator]], and fix a strict meter pair $z_0\prec\prec z_1$ in $\Gamma_m$. Assume the Axiom of Choice. Then one can choose, for every $i\in I$, an additive constant and positive scale for its same-type entropy so that

$$S\big((t_1i_1,x_1),\ldots,(t_ni_n,x_n)\big)=\sum_{\ell=1}^n t_\ell S_{i_\ell}(x_\ell)$$

is additive, extensive, and characterizes every same-composition comparison on every finite separated product. No conclusion is asserted for transitions that change composition.

Let $\mathcal G$ be a set of tagged system types closed under finite composition $T\times T'$ and positive scaling $tT$. Scaling is associative and acts componentwise on products: $s(tT)=(st)T$ and $t(T\times T')=(tT)\times(tT')$. Each type $T$ has a nonempty state set $X_T$ of finite tagged compounds, every state in $X_T$ is represented by the coefficient-map interpretation of [[def-tdmath-forward-sector-hypotheses]] and has the fixed aggregate composition $\nu(a)=\nu_T$ of its declared type, using the amount-function interpretation in [[def-tdmath-forward-sector-hypotheses]], and has total coefficient mass $m(T)=w_T\ge0$, and $\nu_{T\times T'}=\nu_T+\nu_{T'}$, $\nu_{tT}=t\nu_T$, with $m(T\times T')=m(T)+m(T')$ and $m(tT)=t\,m(T)$. Matching scalar masses alone do not identify aggregate composition. The entropy $\sigma_T:X_T\to\mathbb R$ is the finite additive extensive entropy from [[thm-tdmath-arbitrary-family-calibration]]; in particular $\sigma_{tT}(ta)=t\sigma_T(a)$.

Include the formal empty unit type $1$, with $X_1=\{*\}$, $m(1)=0$, $\sigma_1(*)=0$, $T\times1=T$, and $t1=1$. A transition edge from type $T$ to type $T'$ is a pair $a\in X_T$, $b\in X_{T'}$ such that the underlying equal-mass compounds satisfy $a\prec b$ under [[def-tdmath-forward-sector-hypotheses]]. Thus an edge can exist only when $m(T)=m(T')$. Its cost is the finite real number $\sigma_{T'}(b)-\sigma_T(a)$.

A decorated finite chain from $\Gamma$ to $\Gamma'$ consists of a catalyst type $C\in\mathcal G$, an integer $N\ge1$, types $T_0=\Gamma\times C,T_1,\ldots,T_N=\Gamma'\times C$, and states $a_k\in X_{T_k}$, $b_{k+1}\in X_{T_{k+1}}$ with an edge $a_k\prec b_{k+1}$ for every $0\le k<N$. Its cost is the finite real sum

$$c=\sum_{k=0}^{N-1}\bigl(\sigma_{T_{k+1}}(b_{k+1})-\sigma_{T_k}(a_k)\bigr).$$

Define $F(\Gamma,\Gamma')$ as the infimum of all such witness costs. Set $F=+\infty$ if there is no witness and $F=-\infty$ if the witness costs are unbounded below. The infimum is over real witness costs, so no subtraction of extended-real infima is used. Type permutations, reassociation, reversible identifications, and the identity $T\times1=T$ are part of the declared type structure. The cost identities and inequalities require a separate proof.

For the cost $F$ of [[def-tdmath-decorated-chain-costs]], $F(\Gamma,\Gamma)=0$, $F$ is positively homogeneous, invariant under adding the same catalyst to both endpoints, and satisfies the triangle inequality whenever the extended-real sum on its right is defined. It is subadditive under composition whenever $F(\Gamma_1,\Gamma'_1)+F(\Gamma_2,\Gamma'_2)$ is defined. Every pair of actual forward and reverse decorated-chain witnesses has nonnegative total cost. A finite reverse witness therefore bounds all forward costs below; $F=-\infty$ can occur only when the reverse direction has no witness.

Under A1–A6 of [[def-tdmath-forward-sector-hypotheses]], for compounds $A,B$ with $m(A)=m(B)$ and every finite spectator compound $C$, $A+C\prec B+C$ if and only if $A\prec B$. Consequently, for finite-support signed maps $u,v$ of equal total coefficient, define $u\preceq_s v$ by $(v-u)^-\prec(v-u)^+$. This relation is well-defined, agrees with $\prec$ on nonnegative maps, is invariant under adding a common signed map, is transitive, and is closed under addition of two comparisons. No comparison hypothesis is used.
In the complete ordered field $\mathbb R$, the sequence $\epsilon_n:=1/(n+1)$, $n\in\mathbb N$, is positive, strictly decreasing, and converges to zero.

derivations.claim: If $x\prec y$, the one-edge witness with an identity catalyst has cost $\sigma_{\Gamma'}(y)-\sigma_\Gamma(x)$. Hence $F(\Gamma,\Gamma')\le\sigma_{\Gamma'}(y)-\sigma_\Gamma(x)$, which is the forward inequality, including the case $F=+\infty$ where no such transition can exist.

Conversely assume the displayed entropy inequality. It is impossible when $F=+\infty$. For each natural index $n\in\mathbb N$, use $\epsilon_n$ from [F5] and choose a decorated witness of real cost $c_n\le\Delta\sigma+h\epsilon_n$, where $\Delta\sigma=\sigma_{\Gamma'}(y)-\sigma_\Gamma(x)$ and $h=\sigma(z_1)-\sigma(z_0)>0$ is the entropy gap of a fixed strict meter pair from [F1]. Such witnesses exist from the definition of infimum, also if $F=-\infty$. Write their types as $T_0=\Gamma\times C,T_1,\ldots,T_N=\Gamma'\times C$, their edges as $a_k\prec b_{k+1}$, and their endpoints as $a_0=(\widetilde x,c_0)$, $b_N=(\widetilde y,d_0)$.

Put $\delta_n=\epsilon_n$. In one finite compound type form
$L_n=(x,b_N,b_1,\ldots,b_{N-1},\delta_n z_0),\qquad R_n=(a_0,y,a_1,\ldots,a_{N-1},\delta_n z_1).$
These have the same composition: both contain $\Gamma$, $\Gamma'$, the catalyst $C$, every intermediate type $T_1,\ldots,T_{N-1}$, and one scaled meter state, up to reassociation and permutation. Additivity of $\sigma$ and the definition of chain cost give
$\sigma(R_n)-\sigma(L_n)=\Delta\sigma-c_n+\delta_n h\ge0.$
Thus the same-composition entropy representation [F1] gives $L_n\prec R_n$.

Starting from $R_n$, use consistency on $a_0\prec b_1$ with $y,\delta_nz_1,a_1,\ldots,a_{N-1}$ as spectators. The result contains $b_1$ in place of $a_0$. Next use $a_1\prec b_2$ with $y,\delta_nz_1,b_1,a_2,\ldots,a_{N-1}$ as spectators, and continue in order. At stage $k$, the current compound contains $a_k$, the earlier outputs $b_1,\ldots,b_k$, all later inputs $a_{k+1},\ldots,a_{N-1}$, and the unchanged $y,\delta_nz_1$. After the last edge, transitivity gives $R_n\prec R'_n$, where $R'_n=(b_1,\ldots,b_N,y,\delta_nz_1)$. Compose this with $L_n\prec R_n$ from step 2.1. The compounds $L_n$ and $R'_n$ share the finite spectator $b_1+\cdots+b_N$; cancel it by [F4]. The result is $x+\delta_nz_0\prec y+\delta_nz_1$ for every $n$.

By [F5], $\delta_n\downarrow0$, stability in [A1] with bases $x,y$ and fixed positive spectators $z_0,z_1$ yields $x\prec y$. This proves the reverse implication without assuming that any infimum is attained.

Fix a family $I$ of primitive material labels. A tagged type $c\in I$ retains its identity even if another type has the same coordinate domain. A positive scale $\lambda>0$ is dimensionless and is represented by the separately tagged bulk copy $c^{(\lambda)}$ and map $\delta_\lambda$ from [[post-td-bulk-additivity]]. A finite separated compound is a finite tuple of tagged scaled systems, with permutation and reassociation identifications and an empty unit type. Its state is a tuple of constituent equilibrium states; its extensive coordinate tuple is the sum specified by [[post-td-bulk-additivity]] whenever the pair is admitted there.

The formal composition vector of a compound records, for each primitive label $c$, the sum of its positive scale coefficients. Two compounds have the same composition exactly when these vectors agree. The distinct **formal mass** $m(A)$ is the sum of all scale coefficients in $A$, a dimensionless bookkeeping quantity; it is not physical mass in kilograms, mole amount, energy, or volume. Same-composition compounds have equal formal mass. For states $A,B$ of the same compound type, write $A\prec B$ when the declared adiabatic-accessibility relation of [[def-td-adiabatic-accessibility]] admits that endpoint comparison. This definition does not infer accessibility from coordinate addition.

An equal-composition comparison is a comparison between states of types with the same formal composition vector. The later reaction-network definition may separately admit transitions between distinct composition types, but the mathematical supplier still requires equal formal mass at both endpoints. A physical application must state how its channel preserves the chosen formal mass and separately record its dimensioned conservation balances. The empty unit has one state and formal mass zero. No identity is imposed between a primitive type and a scaled tag, or between two different decompositions of a compound, beyond the explicitly declared reassociation, permutation, and bulk-composition maps.

Use thermal joins and $\sim_T$ exactly as defined in [[def-td-thermal-join]]. For every ordered pair of simple systems and every admitted finite join, adopt:

**T1 (joining).** $(x,y)\prec J_{ij}(x,y)$.

**T2 (reversible splitting).** Every join state has at least one split into component states at its stated total energy and work coordinates that is reversible to the join state. Also, for every state $x$ and every $0<t<1$, the equal-state scaled split $(t x,(1-t)x)$ is reversible to $x$.

**T3 (thermal-equilibrium transitivity).** If $x\sim_T y$ and $y\sim_T z$ in the model’s declared contact family, then $x\sim_T z$. This requires the model to provide the relevant joined types and identifications.

**T4 (transversality).** For each simple-system state $x$, there are $x_0,x_1$ in that system with $x_0\prec\prec x\prec\prec x_1$ and $x_0\sim_T x_1$.

The axioms apply to admitted types and their joins only. T4 is an assumption about the contact relation; it is not a consequence of an equation of state or of a thermometer reading. The stronger range condition T5 is stated separately in [[post-td-universal-thermal-range]], and join coherence C1 is separately stated in [[post-td-equilibrium-join-coherence]].

The function $\log:(0,\infty)\to\mathbb R$ is continuous and strictly increasing, is onto $\mathbb R$, and satisfies, for $x,y>0$,
$$\log(xy)=\log x+\log y,\qquad \log(x/y)=\log x-\log y,\qquad \log(1/x)=-\log x.$$
Also $\log 1=0$.

derivations.claim: Start at $(1,3)$. Then $\bar U=2$, every point of $A$ has second coordinate at least $3$, and every point of $B$ has second coordinate at least $2$. A finite convex combination of points whose second coordinates are at least $2$ still has second coordinate at least $2$, because it is the weighted sum of those coordinates with nonnegative weights summing to one. Hence every point in $\operatorname{conv}(A\cup B)$ has second coordinate at least $2$, so $(3,1)$ is not in the forward sector and $(1,3)\not\prec(3,1)$.

In the one-system space, strict accessibility is exactly strict increase of $U$, while thermal equilibrium is equality of normalized energies. If $U_0\prec\prec U\prec\prec U_1$, then $U_0<U<U_1$, so $U_0\ne U_1$ and the two cannot be thermally equivalent. Thus T4 fails.

Start instead at $(3,1)$. Again $\bar U=2$; every point of its $A$ has first coordinate at least $3$, and every point of its $B$ has first coordinate at least $2$. Convex combinations therefore have first coordinate at least $2$, so $(1,3)$ is not accessible from $(3,1)$. The two product states are incomparable, and the comparison hypothesis fails.

The single-system function $S(U)=\log U$ is strictly increasing and represents $U\le U'$. If its additive sum represented product accessibility, the states $(1,3)$ and $(3,1)$ would have equal summed entropy $\log 3$, forcing accessibility both ways. Step 1.1 and step 2.1 show neither direction holds. Therefore this single-system entropy does not represent the product relation. Since the example fails T4 by step 1.2, it does not satisfy the hypotheses of a product-comparison result that includes T4.

Let $X$ be nonempty and suppose its finite-support compounds carry the comparison structure of [[def-tdmath-comparison-and-stability]] over the complete ordered field $\mathbb R$. If there are $x_0,x_1\in X$ with $x_0\preceq x_1$ and not $x_1\preceq x_0$, define $S(x):=\sup L_x$ using [[lem-tdmath-reference-supremum-bounds]]. Then $S:X\to\mathbb R$ is normalized by $S(x_0)=0$, $S(x_1)=1$, and for all equal-mass compounds $A=\sum_i a_i e_{x_i}$ and $B=\sum_j b_j e_{y_j}$,

$$A\preceq B\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad\sum_i a_iS(x_i)\le\sum_j b_jS(y_j).$$

Thus $S$ is an additive extensive representation on finite compounds. If no strict pair exists, CH instead makes every equal-mass pair of compounds equivalent, and any constant state function gives a (degenerate) additive representation. No concavity, continuity, or physical law follows without additional hypotheses.

Let $X$ be a set of state labels. A **tagged scalable compound over $X$** is a function $c:X\to\mathbb R_{\ge0}$ whose support $\operatorname{supp}(c):=\{x\in X:c(x)\ne0\}$ is finite. The coefficient is a dimensionless formal amount; state labels retain their tags, so equal coefficients on different labels do not identify those labels. Compounds are equal exactly when their coefficient functions are equal.

For compounds $c,d$ and $t\ge0$, define composition and nonnegative scaling pointwise by $(c+d)(x):=c(x)+d(x)$ and $(tc)(x):=t c(x)$. The zero function is the empty compound; in particular $0c=0$. Comparison axioms involving scaling still require a strictly positive scalar unless explicitly stated otherwise. The **mass** of $c$ is the finite sum $m(c):=\sum_{x\in\operatorname{supp}(c)}c(x)$. It is dimensionless bookkeeping mass, not thermodynamic mass or energy. The compound is positive when $m(c)>0$.

For every state label $x\in X$, the **unit-state compound** $e_x$ is the coefficient function with $e_x(y)=1$ if $y=x$ and $e_x(y)=0$ otherwise. Its support is $\{x\}$, so it is a tagged compound. In compound comparisons, a state label $x$ denotes $e_x$. Every compound has the canonical finite decomposition $c=\sum_{x\in\operatorname{supp}(c)}c(x)e_x$, with an empty sum when $c=0$; coefficients on this support are strictly positive. The mass-one property $m(e_x)=1$ and the equivalence $m(c)=0\Longleftrightarrow c=0$ are proved in [[lem-tdmath-compound-mass-well-defined]].

The formula for mass is independent of the chosen finite set containing the support, and composition and scaling obey $m(c+d)=m(c)+m(d)$ and $m(tc)=t m(c)$; [[lem-tdmath-compound-mass-well-defined]] proves these assertions.

For every tagged scalable compound $c$, the mass in [[def-tdmath-tagged-scalable-compound]] is independent of the finite summation set used. For any compounds $c,d$ and $t\ge0$, $m(c+d)=m(c)+m(d)$ and $m(tc)=t m(c)$; $m(0)=0$. For every $x\in X$, the unit-state compound $e_x$ has $m(e_x)=1$. A compound has zero mass if and only if it is the empty compound.

Let $m\ge1$, let $q_1,\ldots,q_m\in\mathbb R^d$, and let $a_1,\ldots,a_m\in\mathbb R$. Put

$$\Delta_m=\{\theta\in\mathbb R^m:\theta_i\ge0,\ \sum_{i=1}^m\theta_i=1\},\qquad P:=\left\{\sum_{i=1}^m\theta_iq_i:\theta\in\Delta_m\right\}.$$

Thus $P$ is the finite convex hull of the listed points, defined here as their convex combinations.

For $x\in P$ let $\Theta_x=\{\theta\in\Delta_m:\sum_i\theta_iq_i=x\}$ and define

$$f_{\rm mix}(x)=\min_{\theta\in\Theta_x}\sum_{i=1}^m\theta_i a_i;$$

set $f_{\rm mix}(x)=+\infty$ for $x\notin P$. Then every minimum is attained; $f_{\rm mix}$ is proper, lower semicontinuous, and convex; and it is pointwise greatest among convex functions $h:\mathbb R^d\to\overline{\mathbb R}$ satisfying $h(q_i)\le a_i$ for every $i$. Consequently $f_{\rm mix}=f_{\rm mix}^{**}$. If $p\in\partial f_{\rm mix}(x)$ and $\theta$ is any minimizing mixture for $x$, then every $i$ with $\theta_i>0$ satisfies

$$a_i=\langle p,q_i\rangle-f_{\rm mix}^*(p).$$

Thus all occupied data points $(q_i,a_i)$ lie on one supporting affine hyperplane. The assertion is finite-dimensional and makes no claim about infinite families.

derivations.claim: By [A1] and [L1], each $a_i=S(s_i)$ is finite. For any $\theta\in\Delta_m$, [L2] gives $m(M_\theta)=\sum_i\theta_i m(e_{s_i})=\sum_i\theta_i=1$. If $\theta_i=0$, its term is the empty compound and contributes zero; equivalently omit such terms, leaving only positive coefficients and never applying a positive-scaling comparison axiom at zero. The representation assigns $M_\theta$ the value $V(\theta)=\sum_i\theta_i a_i$. By [A3], its coordinate is $\sum_i\theta_i q_i$. Since the states are distinct, the coefficient of $s_i$ in $M_\theta$ is exactly $\theta_i$, so this parametrization is injective. Hence mixtures in this fixed family with coordinate $x$ correspond exactly to $\theta\in\Theta_x$ from [L3].

The minimum of $V(\theta)$ over those mixtures is therefore $\min_{\theta\in\Theta_x}\sum_i\theta_i a_i=f_{\rm mix}(x)$ by [L3], with $+\infty$ when $\Theta_x$ is empty. Every further conclusion in the Statement follows by applying the corresponding conclusion of [L3] to the same finite data. The point-mass and zero-coefficient cases are supplied by [L2]; the transfer remains conditional on [A1] and [A3] and records no independent acceptance of the draft representation.

citations.quote:
Fix an integer spatial dimension $d\geq 1$, a reference length $\ell_0>0$, and a bounded measurable region $\Lambda\subset\mathbb R^d$ with dimensionless volume $V=|\Lambda|$. Its physical region is $\ell_0\Lambda$. A finite positional configuration of $N$ classical point particles in $\Lambda$ is an unordered simple set $\omega=\{x_1,\ldots,x_N\}\subset\Lambda$; simple means that no point is repeated. Particle number $N$ is a dimensionless nonnegative integer and the physical number density corresponding to $N/V$ is $N/(\ell_0^dV)$.

A pair potential is an even measurable function $\varphi:\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R\cup\{+\infty\}$, where $\varphi(x)$ is the interaction energy in joules at physical displacement $\ell_0x$ and evenness means $\varphi(x)=\varphi(-x)$. For a labelled representative of $\omega$, define the positional pair energy
$$H_N(\omega)=\sum_{1\leq i<j\leq N}\varphi(x_i-x_j),\qquad H_0=H_1=0.$$
If any pair is forbidden by the potential, its energy and hence $H_N$ are $+\infty$. This model contains no kinetic energy, internal molecular coordinates, quantum exchange terms, or external field.

The interaction is stable if there is a constant $B\geq0$, measured in joules, such that $H_N(\omega)\geq-BN$ for every finite simple configuration. It has a regular integrable tail if there are $R>0$ and a nonnegative nonincreasing measurable function $\psi:[R,\infty)\to[0,\infty)$, measured in joules, such that $|\varphi(x)|\leq\psi(|x|)$ for $|x|\geq R$ and
$$\int_R^\infty r^{d-1}\psi(r)\,dr<\infty.$$
A stable potential with this tail condition is the stable regularly tempered class used for the free-cube results on this page. Superstability and a positive divergent core are stronger, separate hypotheses and are not implied by stability.

At temperature $T>0$, write $\beta=(k_BT)^{-1}$ in joules inverse. The activity $z>0$ is dimensionless relative to the reference intensity $\ell_0^{-d}$. A free-wall finite-volume model contains only positions in $\Lambda$ and uses $H_N$ above. A periodic model uses the declared periodic cell and sums its periodic-image pair interactions with each unordered pair counted once. These are distinct boundary preparations. The limits on this page are positional configurational limits and do not by themselves include a momentum integral or a full phase-space energy shell.

For a specified finite region and boundary preparation, take $T>0$, $\beta=(k_BT)^{-1}$, and the positional energy in [[def-td-stable-tempered-continuum-preparation]]. For each fixed $N$, specialize the measurable-model canonical preparation of [[post-td-canonical-sampling]] to the dimensionless positional configuration measure $\mu_{\Lambda,N}$; adopt the law
$$P_{\Lambda,N}^{\mathrm{can}}(d\omega)=Z_{\Lambda,N}^{-1}e^{-\beta H_N(\omega)}\mu_{\Lambda,N}(d\omega),\qquad Z_{\Lambda,N}=\int e^{-\beta H_N}\,d\mu_{\Lambda,N},$$
whenever $0<Z_{\Lambda,N}<\infty$. Separately adopt the grand-canonical law at activity $z>0$ to have weights $z^{N(\omega)}e^{-\beta H_{N(\omega)}(\omega)}$ relative to the same indistinguishable positional measures; its normalizer is $\Xi_\Lambda(z,\beta)=\sum_{N\geq0}z^NZ_{\Lambda,N}$ when finite. Here $z$ is dimensionless relative to the reference intensity in [[post-td-classical-indistinguishable-particle-measure]], and $\alpha=\log z$.

For the controlled positional shell of [[def-td-controlled-fixed-n-energy-shell]], adopt the conditional measure $M_n$ only when its shell has positive finite reference measure. These are probability-law preparations used to define the model. They are not derived from Hamiltonian trajectories, and they do not assert that a laboratory apparatus reaches any of them. The inverse-temperature-zero hard-core continuation is governed separately by [[def-td-retained-hard-core-zero-beta-preparation]].

Use the dimensionless coordinates, simple configurations, and pair potential of [[def-td-stable-tempered-continuum-preparation]]. A sequence $(\Lambda_k)_{k\geq1}$ of bounded measurable regions is van Hove if $|\Lambda_k|\to\infty$ and, for every fixed $s>0$,
$$\frac{|\{x\in\Lambda_k:\operatorname{dist}(x,\partial\Lambda_k)\leq s\}|}{|\Lambda_k|}\longrightarrow0.$$
This is an explicit condition on the boundary-layer volume; increasing volume alone does not imply it. A free wall permits particles only in $\Lambda_k$ and includes no exterior particles. A periodic wall uses the specified periodic cell and its image convention.

For the deterministic exterior class, let $C=[-1/2,1/2)^d$ and $\Lambda_n=[-n-1/2,n+1/2)^d$, with $V_n=|\Lambda_n|$. For a locally finite exterior configuration $\zeta\subset\mathbb R^d$, write $N_{C+i}(\zeta)=|\zeta\cap(C+i)|$. Given $t<\infty$, define
$$\Omega(t)=\left\{\zeta:\sum_{i\in\Lambda_n\cap\mathbb Z^d}N_{C+i}(\zeta)^2\leq tV_n\ \text{for every integer }n\geq0\right\}.$$
For an interior configuration $\omega\subset\Lambda_n$, its exterior interaction is
$$W_n(\omega,\zeta)=\sum_{x\in\omega}\sum_{y\in\zeta\setminus\Lambda_n}\varphi(x-y),$$
interpreted as an extended-real sum. A positive infinite value has zero Boltzmann weight. The regular tail controls distant terms; the class $\Omega(t)$ is a fixed uniform bound on exterior cell counts, not permission for an arbitrary volume-filling external potential. The van Hove and uniformly tempered exterior conditions are separate boundary regimes.

Assume AC, as required by the current mathematical definition and its shape suppliers. Let $d\geq2$, $E_0=1\,\mathrm J$, $\widehat\varphi=\varphi/E_0$, and assume $\widehat\varphi$ is Borel measurable and superstable and regular as in [[def-tdmath-superstable-regular-interaction]]. Use $\widehat H=H/E_0$ and $\widehat\beta=E_0(k_BT)^{-1}>0$ in the mathematical rates. Let $(\Lambda_k)$ be a van Hove sequence as in [[def-td-admissible-van-hove-and-tempered-exterior]]. First, for free walls, the positional grand pressure along $\Lambda_k$ converges to the free-cube pressure of [[pthm-td-stable-tempered-free-cube-grand-pressure]]. For any positive interior attainable density $\rho$ and exact integers $N_k$ with $N_k/|\Lambda_k|\to\rho$, the exact-$N_k$ free-wall canonical log-partition rate converges to the same cube canonical rate. These two shape statements require superstability and regularity; stability alone is not asserted to suffice for arbitrary van Hove shapes.

Second, strengthen the potential hypothesis: for some $r_0>0$, $\widehat\varphi(x)\geq\widehat\chi(\|x\|_\infty)>0$ whenever $0<\|x\|_\infty\leq r_0$, where $\widehat\chi$ is nonincreasing and $\int_0^{r_0}\widehat\chi(r)r^{d-1}\,dr=+\infty$. For each fixed $t<\infty$, the free-wall grand pressure in $\Lambda_n$ with exterior $\zeta\in\Omega(t)$ then converges uniformly in $\zeta$ to the same free-cube pressure. The exterior interaction is the deterministic positional term of [[def-td-admissible-van-hove-and-tempered-exterior]], not a volume-filling external field. This genuine divergent-core condition is the exact stronger hypothesis of the current exterior supplier; it is not inferred from superstability or replaced by a weaker source condition.

derivations.claim: Since $H_N=0$, the finite-volume canonical positional integral is $Z_{V,N}=V^N/N!$. Summing the adopted grand weights gives $\Xi_V=\sum_{N\geq0}(zV)^N/N!=e^{zV}$.

Adding $cN$ to the energy multiplies the $N$-particle weight by $e^{-\beta cN}$, so $\Xi_V^{(c)}=\sum_{N\geq0}(ze^{-\beta c}V)^N/N!=e^{ze^{-\beta c}V}$. For $c\neq0$ this has a different log-partition rate.

The perturbation is a potential on every point of $\Lambda$, whereas [F2] and [L1] restrict the boundary result to free walls or the interaction with one fixed uniformly tempered exterior configuration. Therefore this example lies outside those hypotheses and contradicts no qualified boundary conclusion.

case_scope.source_excerpt: For the ideal positional gas $\varphi=0$ in a region of dimensionless volume $V$, the grand partition is $\Xi_V(z,\beta)=e^{zV}$. Now impose an external energy $c$ joules per particle at every point of the volume. The new grand partition is $\Xi_V^{(c)}=e^{ze^{-\beta c}V}$, so the dimensionless pressure rate changes from $z$ to $ze^{-\beta c}$ when $c\neq0$. This exact volume-filling external preparation is not a member of the deterministic exterior class used by [[pthm-td-qualified-van-hove-and-exterior-limit]].
